I'm not a doctor. I'm not a scientist. I'm a woman at her kitchen table who almost took the same pill her father did, and I need to tell you what I found out too late to tell him.\n\nMy father has been gone for nine years. He died the spring our youngest started kindergarten.\n\nThe year before, he'd started saying his belly felt tight. He was 65. His GP said keep up the MiraLAX, maybe add a little Metamucil. He did. He did exactly what they told him.\n\nThe week he died, I didn't know how bad it had gotten. He hadn't told my mother. He hadn't told me.\n\nThe death certificate said complications from chronic constipation. I didn't understand what that meant. On the flight home from the funeral I made myself read the discharge summary, word by word, until I did.\n\nA stool impaction had blocked his bowel. It sat there long enough that the wall tore. The infection went into his blood. Sepsis. He was 66.\n\nMy father measured things for a living \u2014 thirty-six years a bridge engineer for the state DOT \u2014 and he died on a bathroom floor of constipation.\n\nI know how that sounds. I didn't believe it either, until I read it in a hospital's own words.\n\nEvery test he ever took came back normal.\n\nHe died of the thing they were managing.\n\nThe MiraLAX had shown up on his counter the year I turned 30. His GP had a line for it.\n\n\"This is your new best friend now.\"\n\nMy father wrote it down on a Post-it inside the kitchen cabinet. His engineer's block letters. NEW BEST FRIEND. Underlined once.\n\nI found it years later, cleaning out the house. It's the one thing of his I kept.\n\nFor twelve years he scooped white powder into orange juice at 6:15 in the morning. Same scoop. Same glass. \"Regular as a clock,\" he'd say. Like a small joke. Like a man reporting in from a bridge inspection.\n\nI believed him.\n\nI want to tell you what happened to me before I tell you what I found out. Because if you're a woman around my age reading this, some of it is going to sound like the inside of your own house.\n\nIt started for me a few years after he was gone. I was 45, maybe 46. Every other day. Then every third. Then every fourth. By 48 it was every four or five days at best.\n\nAnd somewhere in there the urge itself went quiet.\n\nI don't know how to describe that to someone who hasn't lived it. I used to at least feel it coming. By 48 I felt nothing. No signal. No warning. Like my body had forgotten how to go on its own. I only went when I made myself go.\n\nThe bloat showed up at 8 PM like a guest who wouldn't leave. I stopped wearing the wrap dress because I looked six months pregnant by dinner. Stopped tucking shirts in. In every photo from those years, I'm pulling a sweater around my waist.\n\nThe strain hour at 6 AM. Door locked. Knees pulled up to my chest. Sixty minutes with my eyes closed while the rest of the house slept.\n\nPebble stools when I did go. Rabbit pellets. One morning there was blood on the paper and I cried in the bathroom for two minutes and then I went to work.\n\nI dread thinking about when I will poop.\n\nI stopped saying that out loud around the time it got bad, because I could hear my mother saying it about my father.\n\nThe drawer.\n\nI stood in front of it one night, in the dark, and made myself list it out loud like naming the dead.\n\nMiraLAX. White powder. Orange juice in the morning.\n\nMetamucil. Three orange tubs stacked in the back.\n\nMagnesium citrate. The green-and-yellow soda bottle. Grapefruit lighter fluid. I'd chug it on Sunday nights.\n\nSenna. The brown tablets. The whip I took the night before a flight.\n\nDulcolax suppositories. The box in the back. The emergency drawer.\n\nMilk of Magnesia. Four months of chalky nightly chugs. Quit working after three rounds.\n\nCastor oil. Once. Three hours of cramping for ten minutes of release. Never again.\n\nAlign. Probiotics. Thirty dollars a month for six months. Three good weeks. Then nothing.\n\nSmooth Move tea. The kettle on at 9 PM every Sunday.\n\nFiber gummies. Two brands. Made the bloat worse.\n\nThe squatty potty under the sink.\n\nA colonoscopy at 41. Nothing remarkable.\n\nI closed the drawer.\n\nStood there.\n\nHalf of those were in my father's cabinet too. Someday one of them is going to clean out my kitchen.\n\nI did not want them finding my Post-it.\n\nThis past spring, around the anniversary of his death, I drove down to help my mother sort my father's old papers.\n\nWe sat at the kitchen table I grew up at.\n\nIn the back of the cabinet, behind the coffee mugs, I found an unopened MiraLAX packet. His. Nine years old.\n\nI held it. And I understood I was standing exactly where he'd stood.\n\nI drove home and booked an appointment with a new doctor \u2014 my old one had retired. I wasn't going for a refill. I think I wanted someone to look at me and tell me I wasn't turning into my father. I made a note in my phone: actually go this time.\n\nThree weeks later I was sitting in Exam Room 4 of the same medical-park complex my father had used for fifteen years.\n\nI didn't realize it at first. Then I saw the framed lithograph of a covered bridge on the wall.\n\nThe same lithograph my father used to make fun of. A bridge engineer, making fun of a bridge lithograph, for fifteen years.\n\nThe chair.\n\nThe vinyl exam chair with the cracked armrest.\n\nThe same chair.\n\nI sat down in it and I could feel my father sitting in it.\n\nMy husband came with me because I'd been crying in the car for two weeks. He sat in the side chair with his hands on his knees.\n\nThe doctor was kind. He was thorough. He listened for six minutes.\n\nThen he reached for his pad and started writing.\n\n\"Let's start you on a daily MiraLAX. It'll be your new best friend.\"\n\nThe same seven words. A different doctor said them to my father in a different room in this same building, twelve years before.\n\nAnd my hand was already moving toward that pad.\n\nI want you to understand that. After the flight home. After the discharge summary. After nine years. My hand was reaching for the same pill that killed him.\n\nThat is how strong the pull is. That is how they get you.\n\nMy husband leaned forward in the side chair. Quiet. Not aggressive. The way he asks the mechanic about the car.\n\n\"Before she starts that \u2014 can somebody actually find out why this keeps happening? Her dad was on that stuff for twelve years.\"\n\nThe doctor paused.\n\nSaid he could refer me to a functional-medicine doctor if I wanted. Didn't push. Pulled a card out of a drawer and handed it to me.\n\nDr. Aurelia Marchetti. Foundation Functional Medicine. On Maple Street.\n\nI took the card. Walked out without starting anything.\n\nThen sat in the parking lot for forty minutes before I could turn the key.\n\nI almost canceled the appointment with Dr. Aurelia twice \u2014 two hundred dollars for an intake form that asks about my father felt like grief tourism. I drove there anyway.\n\nIt's a converted craftsman cottage at the end of Maple Street. Wood floors. A window seat with a wool throw on it. It used to be somebody's dining room and it smells like bergamot tea.\n\nThe receptionist offered me a cup. I drank it.\n\nDr. Aurelia came out herself. Not an assistant. Mid-fifties, gray bob, reading glasses on a beaded chain. She books one patient an hour. I was the patient.\n\nThe intake form was six pages. One whole page about my father.\n\nShe read all of it before she said a word. Then she read my colonoscopy from 41, the bloodwork, the years of nothing remarkable.\n\nShe put it down. \"I'm not going to send you for another scan. You've had them. They're normal.\"\n\nI started to say that was the whole problem. That everything was always normal.\n\nShe nodded before I finished. \"That's the cruel part of this. What's actually wrong doesn't show up on any of them. It didn't show up on your father's either.\"\n\nShe had a little notepad, and she drew a slow line across it.\n\n\"A few times a day, your colon is supposed to squeeze. Hard. One strong contraction that sweeps everything down and out. That squeeze is what you feel as the urge. It's run by a little band of cells in the wall of the colon \u2014 pacemaker cells, the same idea as the ones that keep a heart on beat.\"\n\nShe tapped the line.\n\n\"In someone like you, those cells have been wearing down. For years.\"\n\nI asked her how she could possibly know that. If no scan shows it.\n\n\"Because I've watched it walk through that door a hundred times. Women exactly like you. Every test clean. A little worse every year. And when researchers look at colons like that under a microscope, the cells that fire the squeeze are worn down. What wears them down is oxidation.\"\n\nI asked her what that meant.\n\n\"Rust.\" She saw my face. \"It's the same thing that rusts a piece of steel. Only it's happening to the cells in the wall of your colon. Slowly. Over years.\"\n\nI asked her where it comes from.\n\n\"Your own gut makes it.\"\n\nShe said years of processed food. Years of stress. A course of antibiotics here and there. They wipe out the good bacteria and leave the lining raw and inflamed.\n\nAnd a raw, inflamed lining starts throwing off far too many of these corrosive little molecules. Free radicals, she called them. They don't switch off. Day and night, they wear on those pacemaker cells.\n\nThe cells barely grow back. So the damage stacks up. Year after year.\n\nThe squeeze gets weaker. Then it comes less often. Then it stops coming on its own at all.\n\n\"And one day,\" she said, \"you notice the urge is just gone.\"\n\nThe urge. The thing I'd stopped feeling at 48.\n\n\"You are not broken,\" she said. \"You did not forget how. The cells that run it have been worn down. Quietly. The whole time your tests were coming back normal.\"\n\nShe let that sit.\n\n\"That is why your father's came back normal too. For twelve years.\"\n\nI put my hand over my mouth.\n\nNine years. A death certificate. A discharge summary I made myself read on a plane. And the thing that killed him had been sitting there under every clean test the whole time, and no one ever went looking for it.\n\nShe handed me a tissue from a wooden box on her desk and waited.\n\nI said, \"But they kept telling him more fiber. They told me more fiber too.\"\n\n\"Fiber is a raw ingredient. Your bacteria are supposed to ferment it \u2014 but the same diet that started all this wiped those bacteria out. So the fiber just sits there and turns to gas. That's why it made you more bloated, not less.\" She shrugged. \"You can't eat your way out of cells that are worn down.\"\n\nI started to say something about the laxatives.\n\nShe got there first.\n\n\"A stimulant laxative \u2014 your senna, your Dulcolax \u2014 doesn't fix anything. It lashes your colon into one forced squeeze. That isn't your body doing the work. That's your body being whipped into it. It works once, then it quits, then it needs a bigger dose.\"\n\nShe looked at me.\n\n\"Your father proved his colon could be forced for twelve years. He never once got to find out if it could work on its own.\"\n\nI couldn't answer that.\n\n\"And the MiraLAX,\" she said, \"pulls water in so what's already sitting there slides out. You go, a little. Wet, loose, and still no real urge \u2014 because the squeeze still isn't happening. It clears out today. It does nothing about why your colon stopped doing this on its own.\"\n\nI looked at the wool throw on the window seat across the room and I didn't say anything for a while.\n\nShe let me sit.\n\nThen she said the thing I typed into my phone in the parking lot afterward, the one I've read a hundred times since.\n\n\"You are not your father. You're sitting here. He never got this conversation. You are.\"\n\nNear the end of the hour I asked her the only question left. So what do I actually do.\n\nShe capped her pen. \"That's the hard part. It isn't one job. Soothe that raw lining and put back the good bacteria the modern diet stripped out.\n\nThree. Give the colon back the finished acids it's supposed to make on its own \u2014 the ones that fire the squeeze \u2014 so the urge has a way to come back.\"\n\nShe turned the page toward me.\n\n\"Everything in that drawer of yours was working on what happens downstream. Not one of them stopped the damage, calmed the source, and brought the squeeze back. All three, together.\"\n\nShe said it plainly.\n\n\"The treatments failed you. And the strongest one I keep coming back to for this \u2014 the one that actually goes after these free radicals \u2014 is kombucha.\"\n\nI must have made a face, because she smiled.\n\n\"Not the drink. White powder. Orange juice in the morning.\n\nMetamucil. Three orange tubs stacked in the back.\n\nMagnesium citrate. The green-and-yellow soda bottle. Grapefruit lighter fluid. I'd chug it on Sunday nights.\n\nSenna. The brown tablets. The whip I took the night before a flight.\n\nDulcolax suppositories. The box in the back. The emergency drawer.\n\nMilk of Magnesia. Four months of chalky nightly chugs. Quit working after three rounds.\n\nCastor oil. Once. Three hours of cramping for ten minutes of release. Never again.\n\nAlign. Probiotics. Thirty dollars a month for six months. Three good weeks. Then nothing.\n\nSmooth Move tea. The kettle on at 9 PM every Sunday.\n\nFiber gummies. Two brands. Made the bloat worse.\n\nThe squatty potty under the sink.\n\nA colonoscopy at 41. Nothing remarkable.\n\nI closed the drawer.\n\nStood there.\n\nHalf of those were in my father's cabinet too. I'd been buying them my whole life and not seeing it.\n\nAnd one night it landed on me. I have two kids. Someday one of them is going to clean out my kitchen.\n\nI did not want them finding my Post-it.\n\nThis past spring, around the anniversary of his death, I drove down to help my mother sort my father's old papers.\n\nWe sat at the kitchen table I grew up at.\n\nIn the back of the cabinet, behind the coffee mugs, I found an unopened MiraLAX packet. His. Nine years old.\n\nI held it. And I understood I was standing exactly where he'd stood.\n\nI drove home and booked an appointment with a new doctor \u2014 my old one had retired. I wasn't going for a refill. I think I wanted someone to look at me and tell me I wasn't turning into my father. I made a note in my phone: actually go this time.\n\nThree weeks later I was sitting in Exam Room 4 of the same medical-park complex my father had used for fifteen years.\n\nI didn't realize it at first. Then I saw the framed lithograph of a covered bridge on the wall.\n\nThe same lithograph my father used to make fun of. A bridge engineer, making fun of a bridge lithograph, for fifteen years.\n\nThe chair.\n\nThe vinyl exam chair with the cracked armrest.\n\nThe same chair.\n\nI sat down in it and I could feel my father sitting in it.\n\nMy husband came with me because I'd been crying in the car for two weeks. He sat in the side chair with his hands on his knees.\n\nThe doctor was kind. He was thorough. He listened for six minutes.\n\nThen he reached for his pad and started writing.\n\n\"Let's start you on a daily MiraLAX. It'll be your new best friend.\"\n\nThe same seven words. A different doctor said them to my father in a different room in this same building, twelve years before.\n\nAnd my hand was already moving toward that pad.\n\nI want you to understand that. After the flight home. After the discharge summary. After nine years. My hand was reaching for the same pill that killed him.\n\nThat is how strong the pull is. That is how they get you.\n\nMy husband leaned forward in the side chair. Quiet. Not aggressive. The way he asks the mechanic about the car.\n\n\"Before she starts that \u2014 can somebody actually find out why this keeps happening? Her dad was on that stuff for twelve years.\"\n\nThe doctor paused.\n\nSaid he could refer me to a functional-medicine doctor if I wanted. Didn't push. Pulled a card out of a drawer and handed it to me.\n\nDr. Aurelia Marchetti. Foundation Functional Medicine. On Maple Street.\n\nI took the card. Walked out without starting anything.\n\nThen sat in the parking lot for forty minutes before I could turn the key.\n\nI almost canceled the appointment with Dr. Aurelia twice \u2014 two hundred dollars for an intake form that asks about my father felt like grief tourism. I drove there anyway.\n\nIt's a converted craftsman cottage at the end of Maple Street. Wood floors. A window seat with a wool throw on it. It used to be somebody's dining room and it smells like bergamot tea.\n\nThe receptionist offered me a cup. I drank it.\n\nDr. Aurelia came out herself. Not an assistant. Mid-fifties, gray bob, reading glasses on a beaded chain. She books one patient an hour. I was the patient.\n\nThe intake form was six pages. One whole page about my father.\n\nShe read all of it before she said a word. Then she read my colonoscopy from 41, the bloodwork, the years of nothing remarkable.\n\nShe put it down. \"I'm not going to send you for another scan. You've had them. They're normal.\"\n\nI started to say that was the whole problem. That everything was always normal.\n\nShe nodded before I finished. \"That's the cruel part of this. What's actually wrong doesn't show up on any of them. It didn't show up on your father's either.\"\n\nShe had a little notepad, and she drew a slow line across it.\n\n\"A few times a day, your colon is supposed to squeeze. Hard. One strong contraction that sweeps everything down and out. That squeeze is what you feel as the urge. It's run by a little band of cells in the wall of the colon \u2014 pacemaker cells, the same idea as the ones that keep a heart on beat.\"\n\nShe tapped the line.\n\n\"In someone like you, those cells have been wearing down. For years.\"\n\nI asked her how she could possibly know that. If no scan shows it.\n\n\"Because I've watched it walk through that door a hundred times. Women exactly like you. Every test clean. A little worse every year. And when researchers look at colons like that under a microscope, the cells that fire the squeeze are worn down. What wears them down is oxidation.\"\n\nI asked her what that meant.\n\n\"Rust.\" She saw my face. \"It's the same thing that rusts a piece of steel. Only it's happening to the cells in the wall of your colon. Slowly. Over years.\"\n\nI asked her where it comes from.\n\n\"Your own gut makes it.\"\n\nShe said years of processed food. Years of stress. A course of antibiotics here and there. They wipe out the good bacteria and leave the lining raw and inflamed.\n\nAnd a raw, inflamed lining starts throwing off far too many of these corrosive little molecules. Free radicals, she called them. They don't switch off. Day and night, they wear on those pacemaker cells.\n\nThe cells barely grow back. So the damage stacks up. Year after year.\n\nThe squeeze gets weaker. Then it comes less often. Then it stops coming on its own at all.\n\n\"And one day,\" she said, \"you notice the urge is just gone.\"\n\nThe urge. The thing I'd stopped feeling at 48.\n\n\"You are not broken,\" she said. \"You did not forget how. The cells that run it have been worn down. Quietly. The whole time your tests were coming back normal.\"\n\nShe let that sit.\n\n\"That is why your father's came back normal too. For twelve years.\"\n\nI put my hand over my mouth.\n\nNine years. A death certificate. A discharge summary I made myself read on a plane. And the thing that killed him had been sitting there under every clean test the whole time, and no one ever went looking for it.\n\nShe handed me a tissue from a wooden box on her desk and waited.\n\nI said, \"But they kept telling him more fiber. They told me more fiber too.\"\n\n\"Fiber is a raw ingredient. Your bacteria are supposed to ferment it \u2014 but the same diet that started all this wiped those bacteria out. So the fiber just sits there and turns to gas. That's why it made you more bloated, not less.\" She shrugged. \"You can't eat your way out of cells that are worn down.\"\n\nI started to say something about the laxatives.\n\nShe got there first.\n\n\"A stimulant laxative \u2014 your senna, your Dulcolax \u2014 doesn't fix anything. I have performed seventy-one colectomies in twelve years on women who could not stop straining.\n\nFor twelve years I have been the woman who could not stop straining.\n\nA nurse on my own floor caught me in the stairwell on a Tuesday and asked me a question that ended the lie.\n\nI want to tell you the question.\n\nAnd I want to tell you why a surgeon who removes colons for a living had not, in twelve years, fixed her own.\n\nLet me start with why I do this work.\n\nMy mother was constipated her whole life.\n\nNobody ever figured out why.\n\nBy the time she was sixty-four it had a name, and by the time she was sixty-eight she had a partial colectomy.\n\nShe never got her life back after that.\n\nSo I went into colorectal surgery.\n\nI trained at the best program in the country.\n\nI residency.\n\nYour colon does not move on its own schedule.\n\nIt moves when it gets a chemical signal.\n\nThat signal is made by specific bacteria living in your gut.\n\nThey take what you eat and ferment it into a small family of molecules called short-chain fatty acids.\n\nThree of them matter most.\n\nAcetate.\n\nPropionate.\n\nButyrate.\n\nThose molecules land on a receptor on the cells I'd chug it on Sunday nights.\n\nSenna. The brown tablets. The whip I took the night before a flight.\n\nDulcolax suppositories. The box in the back. The emergency drawer.\n\nMilk of Magnesia. Four months of chalky nightly chugs. Quit working after three rounds.\n\nCastor oil. Once. Three hours of cramping for ten minutes of release. Never again.\n\nAlign. Probiotics. Thirty dollars a month for six months. Three good weeks. Then nothing.\n\nSmooth Move tea. The kettle on at 9 PM every Sunday.\n\nFiber gummies. Two brands. Made the bloat worse.\n\nThe squatty potty under the sink.\n\nA colonoscopy at 41. Nothing remarkable.\n\nI closed the drawer.\n\nStood there.\n\nHalf of those were in my father's cabinet too. I'd been buying them my whole life and not seeing it.\n\nAnd one night it landed on me. I have two kids. Someday one of them is going to clean out my kitchen.\n\nI did not want them finding my Post-it.\n\nThis past spring, around the anniversary of his death, I drove down to help my mother sort my father's old papers.\n\nWe sat at the kitchen table I grew up at.\n\nIn the back of the cabinet, behind the coffee mugs, I found an unopened MiraLAX packet. His. Nine years old.\n\nI held it. And I understood I was standing exactly where he'd stood.\n\nI drove home and booked an appointment with a new doctor \u2014 my old one had retired. I wasn't going for a refill. I think I wanted someone to look at me and tell me I wasn't turning into my father. I made a note in my phone: actually go this time.\n\nThree weeks later I was sitting in Exam Room 4 of the same medical-park complex my father had used for fifteen years.\n\nI didn't realize it at first. Then I saw the framed lithograph of a covered bridge on the wall.\n\nThe same lithograph my father used to make fun of. A bridge engineer, making fun of a bridge lithograph, for fifteen years.\n\nThe chair.\n\nThe vinyl exam chair with the cracked armrest.\n\nThe same chair.\n\nI sat down in it and I could feel my father sitting in it.\n\nMy husband came with me because I'd been crying in the car for two weeks. He sat in the side chair with his hands on his knees.\n\nThe doctor was kind. He was thorough. He listened for six minutes.\n\nThen he reached for his pad and started writing.\n\n\"Let's start you on a daily MiraLAX. It'll be your new best friend.\"\n\nThe same seven words. A different doctor said them to my father in a different room in this same building, twelve years before.\n\nAnd my hand was already moving toward that pad.\n\nI want you to understand that. After the flight home. After the discharge summary. After nine years. My hand was reaching for the same pill that killed him.\n\nThat is how strong the pull is. That is how they get you.\n\nMy husband leaned forward in the side chair. Quiet. Not aggressive. The way he asks the mechanic about the car.\n\n\"Before she starts that \u2014 can somebody actually find out why this keeps happening? Her dad was on that stuff for twelve years.\"\n\nThe doctor paused.\n\nSaid he could refer me to a functional-medicine doctor if I wanted. Didn't push. Pulled a card out of a drawer and handed it to me.\n\nDr. Aurelia Marchetti. Foundation Functional Medicine. On Maple Street.\n\nI took the card. Walked out without starting anything.\n\nThen sat in the parking lot for forty minutes before I could turn the key.\n\nI almost canceled the appointment with Dr. Aurelia twice \u2014 two hundred dollars for an intake form that asks about my father felt like grief tourism. I drove there anyway.\n\nIt's a converted craftsman cottage at the end of Maple Street. Wood floors. A window seat with a wool throw on it. It used to be somebody's dining room and it smells like bergamot tea.\n\nThe receptionist offered me a cup. I drank it.\n\nDr. Aurelia came out herself. Not an assistant. Mid-fifties, gray bob, reading glasses on a beaded chain. She books one patient an hour. I was the patient.\n\nThe intake form was six pages. One whole page about my father.\n\nShe read all of it before she said a word. They're normal.\"\n\nI started to say that was the whole problem. That everything was always normal.\n\nShe nodded before I finished. \"That's the cruel part of this. What's actually wrong doesn't show up on any of them. It didn't show up on your father's either.\"\n\nShe had a little notepad, and she drew a slow line across it.\n\n\"A few times a day, your colon is supposed to squeeze. Hard. One strong contraction that sweeps everything down and out. That squeeze is what you feel as the urge. It's run by a little band of cells in the wall of the colon \u2014 pacemaker cells, the same idea as the ones that keep a heart on beat.\"\n\nShe tapped the line.\n\n\"In someone like you, those cells have been wearing down. For years.\"\n\nI asked her how she could possibly know that. If no scan shows it.\n\n\"Because I've watched it walk through that door a hundred times. Women exactly like you. Every test clean. A little worse every year. And when researchers look at colons like that under a microscope, the cells that fire the squeeze are worn down. What wears them down is oxidation.\"\n\nI asked her what that meant.\n\n\"Rust.\" She saw my face. \"It's the same thing that rusts a piece of steel. Only it's happening to the cells in the wall of your colon. Slowly. Over years.\"\n\nI asked her where it comes from.\n\n\"Your own gut makes it.\"\n\nShe said years of processed food. Years of stress. A course of antibiotics here and there. They wipe out the good bacteria and leave the lining raw and inflamed.\n\nAnd a raw, inflamed lining starts throwing off far too many of these corrosive little molecules. Free radicals, she called them. They don't switch off. Day and night, they wear on those pacemaker cells.\n\nThe cells barely grow back. So the damage stacks up. Year after year.\n\nThe squeeze gets weaker. Then it comes less often. Then it stops coming on its own at all.\n\n\"And one day,\" she said, \"you notice the urge is just gone.\"\n\nThe urge. The thing I'd stopped feeling at 48.\n\n\"You are not broken,\" she said. \"You did not forget how. The cells that run it have been worn down. Quietly. The whole time your tests were coming back normal.\"\n\nShe let that sit.\n\n\"That is why your father's came back normal too. For twelve years.\"\n\nI put my hand over my mouth.\n\nNine years. A death certificate. A discharge summary I made myself read on a plane. And the thing that killed him had been sitting there under every clean test the whole time, and no one ever went looking for it.\n\nShe handed me a tissue from a wooden box on her desk and waited.\n\nI said, \"But they kept telling him more fiber. They told me more fiber too.\"\n\n\"Fiber is a raw ingredient. Your bacteria are supposed to ferment it \u2014 but the same diet that started all this wiped those bacteria out. career.\n\nEvery week, I prep bodies for the table. I clean them out. I watch the scope go in. And I write up what the doctor finds, in the language he tells me to use. The note that goes in the chart. The note that tells the patient why they're still backed up. The note that closes the visit.\n\nFor 23 years, I've been writing the wrong thing.\n\nNot because I don't know the truth. Because I do.\n\nI see it almost every time. A colon that has gone quiet. Stool sitting in the upper bend for days, dried to pebbles, where the wave should have carried it out. A muscle that has simply stopped getting the message to move.\n\nAnd we write \"clean scope.\" We write \"no obstruction.\" We write \"irritable bowel \u2014 try more fiber.\"\n\nWe never write what's actually wrong.\n\nNot once. In 23 years. In over 6,000 charts.\n\nAnd I need to tell you about the one that broke me.\n\nHer name was Margaret.\n\nMargaret was 52. Married to a high school football coach named Dean. Two grown kids. Taught fourth grade for 24 years. Sang in her church choir. The kind of person an entire town shows up for when something goes wrong.\n\nSomething went wrong.\n\nShe'd been to her doctor for five years. Always the same complaints. Bloated so hard by every evening she looked six months pregnant. Straining until she sweat, then nothing. Going eleven days without a real bowel movement, then a cramp that doubled her over.\n\nHer doctor said IBS. Then stress. Then perimenopause. Then \"this is just what happens in your early 50s.\"\n\nFive years of visits. Five years of being told nothing was wrong.\n\nMargaret ended up in the ER on a Thursday afternoon. Her husband drove her in. She'd come home from school early because she couldn't stand up straight.\n\nDiagnosis on the ER chart: fecal impaction. Bowel completely backed up.\n\nShe landed on our floor the following Monday for a clean-out and a scope.\n\nI prepped her myself. Standard procedure. We cleaned her out.\n\nAnd I stopped.\n\nHer colon was stretched to nearly twice the size it should have been. The wall was thin and slack, the way it gets when a muscle has not done its job in a very long time.\n\nAnd the whole stretch of it \u2014 the bend, the lower loop \u2014 sat silent. No wave. No tone. Stool packed in where the signal should have carried it through years ago.\n\nI've learned to recognize that after 23 years.\n\nI leaned in while the doctor read the screen.\n\nA colon that had simply stopped getting told to move. For so long the muscle had gone slack. The kind of slow, quiet failure you don't see on a single test \u2014 you only see it when you've watched a thousand of them.\n\nHer colon didn't quit because it was old. It quit because it had stopped getting the one signal that tells it to push.\n\nI stood there for a long time. Looking at Margaret's chart. A 52-year-old fourth grade teacher who sang in the choir and went to the ER because her own body had stopped doing the one thing every body is built to do.\n\nAnd I knew exactly why.\n\nI wrote \"clean scope, no obstruction\" in the note.\n\nI didn't mention the dead-quiet wall. I just left out the part about why the colon had quit anyway.\n\nAnd I would have kept doing it.\n\nUntil Karen.\n\nKaren is my wife.\n\nWe've been married for 22 years. She's 53. Healthy. Active. The kind of person who's never missed a day of work.\n\nAbout a year ago, she started complaining about bloating after meals. Nothing dramatic. Just enough to notice. A signal that quietly went silent. Invisible to every standard test the system runs.\n\nThe tests aren't built to measure this.\n\nI knew Karen's colon had gone quiet. No disease to blame. No tumor to take out. Just my own body, quietly quitting, and not one person able to tell me why.\n\nThen about five months ago, something happened.\n\nI was prepping a patient \u2014 Eileen, lovely woman, early sixties \u2014 for a gallbladder removal. Making small talk to settle her before the anesthesia.\n\nShe said she'd been dreading it because her gut had \"been a wreck for years,\" and she was sure the whole thing would set her off.\n\n\"Used to be, anyway,\" she said.\n\nMy hands paused over her IV line.\n\n\"Used to be?\"\n\nShe smiled. \"Couldn't go for a week at a time. Lived on laxatives. So bloated a coworker once asked me when I was due.\" She laughed at herself. \"Found something that actually works. A kombucha gummy. But not the drink \u2014 I tried the drink, did nothing, just gave me gas. This one was different.\"\n\nI must have looked skeptical, because she laughed again.\n\n\"I know. I know exactly how I sound. I said the same thing when my daughter told me. But honey \u2014 I go every morning now. On my own. First time in years I'm not living on Miralax.\"\n\nI finished prepping her. The gallbladder came out clean. But I couldn't stop thinking about what she'd said.\n\nThat night I sat down at my computer and started reading. Not blog posts. The actual studies.\n\nAnd the first thing I read explained something 23 years of nursing never had.\n\nRemember when your body just told you it was time? When you got the urge on its own \u2014 and you went, without thinking about it, without taking anything?\n\nI couldn't remember the last time I'd felt that. Mine used to come first thing in the morning \u2014 yours might've been different, everyone's is \u2014 but you know the feeling I mean. And it's gone.\n\nIt turns out that feeling has a mechanism, and losing it isn't your colon being broken.\n\nYour colon doesn't squeeze stool along an inch at a time. Once or twice a day \u2014 usually after a meal \u2014 it's supposed to fire one big wave. A single sweep that pushes everything toward the exit. That sweep is the urge. When the wave stops firing, the urge disappears, and the stool just sits there long enough to dry out and turn into exactly what I was straining over.\n\nAnd the wave only fires when it gets a chemical go-signal \u2014 a set of acids your gut bacteria make when they ferment what you eat. Mine had gone quiet. Years of processed food, a couple of rounds of antibiotics, the low-grade inflammation that settles into a gut worn down like that, getting older \u2014 the bacteria that make that signal get starved out, the acids drop off, and the wave stops coming.\n\nMy colon was never broken. It had stopped getting the signal.\n\nAnd not one thing I'd taken in fifteen years was the signal. Fiber, magnesium, Miralax, Dulcolax \u2014 they add bulk, or pull water, or force one contraction. None of them is the thing that fires the wave.\n\nThat was the moment fifteen years of \"drink more water, eat more fiber, push harder\" fell apart in my hands.\n\nReal research. Peer-reviewed. Not blog posts.\n\nThen I read about fermented kombucha. The acids in it are the same ones the wave runs on. In one trial, people went 42\u0025 more often in ten days. Not forced. Fed.\n\nAnd I'd actually tried kombucha. Months back. A bottle from the grocery cooler. It did nothing but bloat me, and I'd written the whole idea off.\n\nBut the more I read, the more I noticed something. People weren't saying \"kombucha works.\" They were very specific. Most of it did nothing, they said \u2014 something about the dose.\n\nSo I dug in. And my stomach dropped.\n\nThe drink was never a dose. It isn't standardized. When a lab tested store kombucha, the acids that actually do the work \u2014 acetic, gluconic, glucuronic \u2014 were missing entirely from half the brands, and what was there swung wildly from one bottle to the next. Most of it is still fermenting on the shelf: barely any live culture left, more alcohol than the label admits, more gas in a gut that's already bloated. You'd have to drink several bottles a day to get near what the studies used.\n\nNo wonder the bottle I tried did nothing. I'd had the right idea and the wrong thing in my hand \u2014 same as the fiber, same as all of it.\n\nThen I remembered Eileen had been specific. She'd said most of them were useless \u2014 it was one in particular. He's a building inspector. He sat in the side chair with his hands on his knees.\n\nHe leaned forward. Quiet. The way he reads a contract before he signs it.\n\n\"Before she fills it \u2014 can someone look at what's actually broken? One whole page about my father.\n\nThe receptionist offered me a cup of tea. I drank it.\n\nDr. Nguyen came out herself to call my name. Mid-fifties. She booked one patient an hour. Color-coded bars across the screen, like a soundboard.\n\nShe pointed at the first one.\n\n\"This is your Bifidobacterium. That's the gap the laxative can't close.\"\n\nThere it was.\n\nThe answer to the question I'd carried since I was 33, standing in a hospital hallway being told my father was gone.\n\nHis output was managed for twelve years. And he still died of what the laxative was supposed to prevent.\n\n\"So is the laxative my only option?\" I asked.\n\n\"You have two paths,\" she said.\n\n\"Path one. You start the MiraLAX. I run it for a living.\n\nYour doctor almost certainly never ordered it.\n\nI'm Reyna. Nineteen years on a lab bench in Mesa, Arizona. I'm the one who counts the bacteria in your gut.\n\nAnd I'm not supposed to be talking to you at all.\n\nHere's how it works where I am.\n\nYou see a doctor. They draw blood, or they hand you a kit, and somewhere on a form a box gets checked. That sample gets boxed up and shipped to a place like mine \u2014 a reference lab, the building your clinic sends things to when the test is too specialized to run in-house.\n\nI'm the person who runs it.\n\nI load the plate. I run the sequencer. I read the bars that come up on my screen, and I sign the report.\n\nThen the report goes back to the doctor who ordered it. Not to you. Never to you.\n\nTechs don't talk to patients. We don't even know your name half the time \u2014 just a number on a requisition slip. We're the back of the house. You never see us.\n\nI'm breaking that rule today. I'll tell you why in a minute. First I need you to see what I see.\n\nWhen a gut sample comes through for one of the bigger panels \u2014 the ones that actually map the bacteria living in your colon \u2014 the report has blocks.\n\nOne block is the bugs that keep things calm. One block is the troublemakers. And one block, the one I watch, is the acid-makers.\n\nThese are the bacteria that take what you eat and ferment it down into tiny organic acids. Those acids are not waste. They are a signal. They're the chemical message that tells your colon to squeeze.\n\nOn my screen they show up as bars against a line \u2014 the reference range, where a healthy gut should sit.\n\nAnd here is the thing I have watched happen, over and over, for nineteen years.\n\nOn the samples that come in flagged for chronic constipation, that block is on the floor.\n\nThe acid-maker bars sit way down under the line. Sometimes barely there at all.\n\nMeanwhile the rest of the report can look fine. The colonoscopy came back clean. The bloodwork came back clean. By every test the doctor actually ran, nothing is wrong.\n\nBut nobody ran the test that shows the bars on the floor.\n\nBecause that panel \u2014 the one that would explain the whole thing \u2014 is a send-out. Most family doctors never order it. Insurance fights it. It runs you a few hundred dollars out of pocket.\n\nSo it doesn't get ordered.\n\nThe one number your doctor does watch is how often you go. And they watch that number quietly cross a line \u2014 every four days, then every week, then longer \u2014 and when it gets bad enough, they reach into a drawer and hand you the same thing they hand everyone.\n\n\"Take MiraLAX. It'll be your new best friend.\"\n\nMore fiber. More water. More prunes.\n\nAnd the block that would have explained all of it was never on the slip.\n\nThat's the part that started keeping me up.\n\nI'd see the collapse on my screen at 9 a.m. and know there was a real person on the other end of that number \u2014 at home, dreading the bathroom, convinced their body was just broken \u2014 being told to eat more fiber.\n\nAnd I couldn't say a word. The report goes to the doctor. Not to them.\n\nI want to tell you about the drawer.\n\nNot mine. Senna tablets for the desperate weeks.\n\nPrune juice until the smell of it made her gag.\n\nFiber gummies that, near as anyone could tell, made the bloat worse.\n\nA whole shelf of things that worked for exactly one week and then quit.\n\nAnd I knew \u2014 from the bars on my screen \u2014 exactly why every single one of those failed.\n\nFiber needs those acid-making bacteria to do anything. If they're gone, the fiber just sits there. Piles up. Makes the bloat worse, not better.\n\nMiraLAX doesn't restore the signal. It drags water into the colon to force one flush. The waste moves from pressure, not because anything contracted. Then it's over, and you're back where you started.\n\nProbiotics? They send a couple of strains in that mostly wash right through. A capsule of two bugs can't replace the whole acid-making community that thinned out.\n\nEvery one of those is working on the surface. Not one of them touches the block on the floor.\n\nNow I'll tell you why I'm breaking the rule.\n\nMy mother. Estela.\n\nFor years it was \"more prunes, mija, drink more water.\" MiraLAX with her coffee. Those cells release serotonin. The serotonin fires the urge \u2014 and the squeeze that moves things along.\n\nWhen the acid-makers thin out, fewer acids get made. The signal goes faint. The urge fades.\n\nYour colon muscle isn't broken. It's sitting there, perfectly able, waiting for a message that isn't coming.\n\nThat's why people say they \"lost the urge.\" That's why they say \"my body forgot how to go.\"\n\nIt didn't forget. It went quiet.\n\nAnd once I understood that, I had one question \u2014 the same one I ask about anything before I'll trust it: where's the data?\n\nI don't take supplements on faith. A slick coating that won't quite flush.\n\nIt looks like hemorrhoids that bleed onto the paper.\n\nIt looks like a small tear that reopens every Tuesday and Friday.\n\nIt looks like a stomach that is flat at seven in the morning and looks four months pregnant by seven at night.\n\nIt looks like the slow forgetting of what the urge to go even feels like.\n\nYou used to know it. Years ago, before all of this, your body would whisper to you. A small pressure. A small signal. You would know.\n\nBy twenty-two years in, that signal is gone.\n\nYour body has forgotten how to call you.\n\nYou go because the clock says it is morning, not because anything inside you is asking.\n\nYou don't feel like a person until something moves.\n\nThat is the sentence I would say in my head every morning, sitting there, watching the steam come off my coffee on the counter.\n\nI don't feel like a person until something moves.\n\n---\n\nI had tried everything.\n\nI had tried Miralax for ten straight years.\n\nI had tried magnesium citrate. Worked for a week. Then nothing.\n\nI had tried magnesium glycinate.\n\nI had tried prune juice every morning for six months. The smell still turns my stomach.\n\nI had tried bran. Psyllium. Oat fiber. Ground flax.\n\nI had tried eating eighteen grams of fiber at breakfast.\n\nIt made the bloating worse. Not better. Worse.\n\nI had tried Senokot, Dulcolax, castor oil, Smooth Move tea.\n\nI had tried Milk of Magnesia. Got a huge bloated belly. Stopped.\n\nI had tried Align. Culturelle. Fiber gummies from the supermarket. Three different probiotics from the health-food store down the street.\n\nI had tried six weeks of pelvic floor PT.\n\nI had tried, in the bathroom, the small thumb maneuver against the wall that some women learn to do when nothing else works.\n\nI had tried, twelve times, the protocol some woman on the internet said had fixed her in two weeks.\n\nI had tried everything anyone had ever told me to try.\n\nNone of it had given me back the signal to go.\n\n---\n\nI almost didn't book the colonoscopy.\n\nMy sister had had one polyp removed the year before, and her doctor's office had sent her a reminder card to share with family.\n\nThe card sat on my kitchen counter for two weeks.\n\nI thought about throwing it out.\n\nI thought, what is there even to find. I am the most predictable bowel in Western Pennsylvania. Once a morning, with help.\n\nI called and booked anyway.\n\nI thought I would be in and out by lunch.\n\nI thought I would hear \"everything looks fine, see you in ten years.\"\n\n---\n\nI want to tell you about the room.\n\nIt was small. The kind of man who is tired in a careful way, not a sloppy one.\n\nHe pulled up a stool. He sat.\n\nHe looked at me, and then past me, at the door.\n\n\"Is your husband in the waiting room?\" he asked. \"I'd like him in the room for this.\"\n\nThat was the sentence.\n\nThat was the sentence that moved me from the story I had walked in with to a different one.\n\n\"I'd like him in the room for this.\"\n\nA nurse went out and brought Don back. Don sat in the second chair, knees almost touching mine, holding his ball cap in his hands.\n\nDr. Albright turned the monitor toward us.\n\nHe had already pulled up six stills. Three over three. A healthy colon on one side of the screen for comparison. Mine on the other.\n\nI knew which one was mine before he told me.\n\nMine was wider.\n\nA lot wider.\n\nHe said it plainly.\n\n\"Your colon is twice the diameter it should be. This is what twenty-two years of straining looks like.\"\n\nI did not say anything.\n\nDon did not say anything.\n\nDr. Albright let the silence sit.\n\nThen he picked up my discharge sheet, turned it over, took a pen out of his coat pocket, and started to draw.\n\n---\n\n\"Think of it like geological strata,\" he said.\n\nHe drew a thin line across the top of the paper. Then a slightly thicker one below it. Then a thicker one below that. A ladder of widening bands.\n\n\"Every year your colon stretched a little more because the signal to contract wasn't firing. You bore down. The colon didn't push back. It widened instead. Each year is a layer. The colon you have today is the sum of all twenty-two layers.\"\n\nHe looked up.\n\n\"It will not go back. The strata don't unstack.\"\n\nI felt something cold open in the bottom of my stomach.\n\nHe saw my face.\n\n\"It can be stopped,\" he said. \"The strata can stop accumulating. The next ten years of your life can look very different from the last twenty-two if we restart the signaling.\"\n\nI asked him the obvious question.\n\n\"What signaling.\"\n\nHe set the pen down.\n\n\"Your colon doesn't move on its own. It contracts when it gets a chemical signal. The signal is three short-chain fatty acids \u2014 butyrate, acetate, propionate. They tell the colon when to contract.\"\n\nHe paused.\n\n\"In your case, the signal does not arrive. We can see it on the scope. We can see it on the dilation. We can see it in the way your bowel is sitting today. The chemicals that should be telling it to fire are not being made in your gut in any meaningful amount.\"\n\nHe added, briefly: \"Those chemicals normally come from gut bacteria \u2014 yours have been depleted for decades. Probably antibiotics in your thirties for postpartum stuff. Probably Western eating. Doesn't really matter at this point. What matters is the signal isn't there.\"\n\nI asked the question every woman in my position asks.\n\n\"But I eat eighteen grams of fiber at breakfast.\"\n\nHe nodded. Adding more fiber to a colon that can't ferment it is what has been making the bloating worse. Not better. The next ten years can look very different from the last twenty-two if we restart the signaling.\"\n\n---\n\nHe picked the pen back up and wrote three words on the back of my discharge sheet.\n\nPRE-FERMENTED KOMBUCHA.\n\nSLIPPERY ELM BARK.\n\nDANDELION ROOT.\n\nHe turned the paper around so I could read it.\n\n\"Pre-fermented,\" he said. \"That is the important word. He built the kitchen table I grew up eating at.\n\nThe MiraLAX showed up on his counter the year I turned 30.\n\nHis doctor called it the gold standard. Gentle. Magnesium citrate that worked for a month and then needed a bigger dose and then I read it weakens the colon and got scared.\n\nPrune juice by the bottle. Smooth Move tea that just made the same boulder angrier. Senokot, which worked and then quit. Align for six months \u2014 the bottle emptied and nothing else did.\n\nPsyllium in a smoothie that tasted like wet paper, which my sister swore by, which made the bloating worse. I read later that fiber can do that. I read a lot of things later.\n\nAnd the whole time, I'd been checked. Colonoscopy, normal. CT, normal. Bloodwork, fine, fine, fine. Every one of them used \"everything looks normal\" as the reason to send me home with the same three words: fiber, water, Miralax.\n\nI'd get out to my car in the parking lot and just sit there and stare at the wheel. They told me I was fine for ten years. I knew I wasn't.\n\nBy the time I packed for Tokyo I'd stopped thinking about it the way a person should. I put a fresh box of Miralax in my carry-on. Three bottles of magnesium citrate in the checked bag, in case the airport scanner gave me grief. And a bulb syringe at the bottom of a toiletry bag, inside a sandwich bag, the way you pack a thing you'd rather your grown daughter never find.\n\nThe drawer had just become the suitcase. I'd been doing it so long I'd stopped expecting it to ever be any different. This is just how I am \u2014 that was the sentence I lived inside.\n\nI landed on a Tuesday. The first few days I had the bloat I always had \u2014 the brick under my ribs by evening, the jeans left unbuttoned at dinner, the six-months-pregnant look in the mirror of my daughter's tiny bathroom \u2014 and I told myself it was the flight.\n\nDay four nothing came, so I took two Miralax instead of one and drank more water and told myself the sushi was sitting funny. I was on her bathroom floor \u2014 Tokyo small, the whole room the size of a closet \u2014 cheek against the cold tile, and I could not get up. My belly was hard as a countertop and swollen tight, the kind of hard where you press and your hand just bounces back.\n\nMy daughter found me down there. She got on the floor and said my name, and when I couldn't get a word out past the pain \u2014 that's what made her reach for her phone. I'd never heard her that scared, not when she was small, not ever. I might have been.\n\nThe paramedics came in eight minutes. They took one look at my stomach and their faces changed. My daughter translated.\n\nThe doctor told her I had one of the worst impactions he'd seen \u2014 the packed colon had pressed on my bladder hard enough to block it off, which was why I couldn't pee, and a nurse drained two cupfuls with a catheter while I cried.\n\nThe imaging, which I never actually saw \u2014 my daughter told me about it afterward in the hallway with her arms wrapped around herself \u2014 showed I was close to a rupture, and a rupture, the doctor said, would have gone septic, and septic would have been a different conversation.\n\nMy husband was on the phone from home, six time zones back, and he couldn't get a flight out until morning. His voice did the thing voices do when a man is frightened and trying hard not to be \u2014 it cracked once and then went very flat and calm \u2014 and he just kept saying he was there, he was right there, like he could hold me through the phone.\n\nThey gave me an enema, and then the doctor put on a glove and did the rest by hand, and my daughter held my other hand the whole time. I'm ashamed to even be telling you that part. I'm telling you anyway, because somebody reading this is sitting on her own bathroom floor right now and nobody ever told her how far this can actually go.\n\nI survived. They kept me two nights for the fluids and discharged me Sunday morning, into a Tokyo I couldn't pretend I was visiting anymore. Over constipation.\n\nThree days later my daughter took me to another doctor. She'd asked around her office \u2014 a co-worker's mother had seen a man who, the co-worker said, \"helped her with something the regular hospital wouldn't.\"\n\nThe clinic was up a narrow stairwell above a stationery shop, a little waiting room with green chairs and a diagram of the gut on the wall, English on the left and Japanese on the right. He was a gut-motility specialist \u2014 a neurogastroenterologist, my daughter said, handing me his card. Dr. Tanaka.\n\nI'll be honest, I only went because she asked me to. They'd all been very polite and they'd all been wrong.\n\nHe didn't say much for the first twenty minutes. Then he said, \"Your colon isn't broken. The cells that fire its push are.\"\n\nHe drew it for me on a piece of paper, slow, in careful English. A few times a day the colon is supposed to fire one strong contraction, he said \u2014 that contraction is the urge, the push I used to feel \u2014 and it's fired by a tiny set of cells in the wall of the colon, pacemaker cells, delicate ones.\n\nAnd in a modern gut \u2014 decades of processed food, stress, antibiotics \u2014 the colon starts throwing off its own free radicals, little damaging molecules. They've measured it, he said: in people with exactly this kind of constipation, those little factories run far hotter than they should.\n\nDay after day, year after year, they wear the pacemaker cells down. Oxidation, he said, is really just rust \u2014 the same slow thing that eats away a pipe \u2014 except here it was eating at the cells that fire my colon's push.\n\nI wrote some of it on the back of a receipt I had in my bag \u2014 interstitial something, the cells were called \u2014 because I knew the words would be gone by the time we reached the street.\n\n\"And this is why every test came back normal,\" he said. \"The damage is at the level of the cells. It does not show on a colonoscopy. It does not show on a CT. There is no scan for it. So you were told for ten years that nothing was wrong, while the thing that was actually wrong kept getting worse.\"\n\nHe looked at me. \"You didn't lose the urge because you forgot how to go. You lost it because the cells that fire the push got worn down, a little at a time. The push got weaker. Then rarer. Then it stopped.\"\n\nAnd then he said the thing I hadn't let myself hope for. Those cells aren't dead, he said \u2014 worn down, struggling, but not gone \u2014 and once you take away what's been wearing them, the contraction can start firing again.\n\nHe'd watched it happen in his own patients for fifteen years. Slowly, quietly, but it came back. The cells are real, he said. The damage is real. And stopping it is real. What nobody back home had done was put the whole thing into one thing a person could take every day.\n\nI'd spent ten years thinking I was broken and he'd spent twenty minutes showing me I wasn't, and I let myself believe it might be true \u2014 which I hadn't let myself do in a long time.\n\nI asked him what you actually do about it. With food that is already alive.\"\n\nI sat there staring at her. I have a PhD in gut physiology. I have 12 years of laboratory research. I've published papers on colonic signaling and motility failure.\n\nAnd this 94-year-old woman just described the exact limitation of every laxative on the market that I've been documenting in my research for over a decade. In one sentence. Like it was obvious.\n\n\u2014\n\nShe gets up and goes to a shelf near the stove. I will tell you exactly what happened and exactly what we learned from the man who saved her life.\n\n\u2014\n\nI'm 52.\n\nMy wife Joanne is 47.\n\nWe have been married twenty-two years. Two adult kids, one in grad school, one teaching at a high school in another state.\n\nJoanne started a GLP-1 medication nine weeks before the night this happened. Her primary care doctor had prescribed it for her A1C, which had crept into pre-diabetic territory at her annual physical.\n\nShe had also wanted to lose forty pounds for years. The medication was supposed to do both.\n\nIn the first nine weeks she lost fourteen pounds. The food noise in her head \u2014 the thing she had been trying to describe to me for two decades and had finally given up explaining \u2014 went quiet for the first time in her adult life.\n\nShe said it was like someone had turned down a radio that had been on in her head since college.\n\nI want all of that on the record before I tell you the rest, because the medication did do what it was supposed to do.\n\nIt is what it did to her gut, silently, that I am writing about.\n\n\u2014\n\nFor nine weeks, she had been mildly constipated.\n\nGoing every four or five days instead of every day.\n\nShe had taken Miralax twice that week. She had mentioned to me at breakfast that her stomach felt \"heavier than usual\" but she had not used the word pain.\n\nI want to say that again.\n\nFor nine weeks, no real warning. No emergency, no impaction, no ER trip, no bathroom-floor moment.\n\nJust a slow, quiet slowdown that we both wrote off as a side effect she would adjust to.\n\n\u2014\n\nThe Saturday evening this happened was the Saturday before our daughter's birthday.\n\nWe were at the kitchen table eating roast chicken and roasted potatoes that I had made.\n\nJoanne put her fork down halfway through her plate and put one hand on her lower right side.\n\nShe said: \"Something is wrong.\"\n\nShe did not look scared yet. Just confused.\n\nShe said the pain was in her lower right abdomen, sharp, \"like someone was twisting a knife slowly.\"\n\nWe thought appendicitis.\n\nI drove her to the closest hospital, fifteen minutes away.\n\n\u2014\n\nThe first ER did a quick exam.\n\nThe doctor on shift was a man maybe ten years younger than us. He pressed on her stomach. He asked when she had last eaten. He ran basic bloodwork.\n\nHe came back two hours later and said the bloodwork was fine, the rebound test was inconclusive, it was probably \"muscular or possibly an early UTI.\"\n\nHe prescribed her a painkiller and an antibiotic for the possible UTI.\n\nHe sent us home.\n\n\u2014\n\nI do not blame him.\n\nI have thought about him a hundred times since and I have decided that he was doing the best he could with what he was trained to look for.\n\nWhat he was not trained to look for was a slowly perforating colon in a woman nine weeks into a GLP-1 medication.\n\nAlmost nobody is, yet.\n\n\u2014\n\nWe got home around 1 AM.\n\nI helped Joanne into bed.\n\nI gave her the painkiller.\n\nShe fell asleep around 2.\n\nAt 3:14 AM she woke me up by getting out of bed and trying to walk to the bathroom.\n\nShe did not make it to the door.\n\nShe vomited on the carpet.\n\nShe tried to stand back up and her knees gave out.\n\nShe was white. Whiter than I have ever seen her. I remember her saying, twice, \"I am so sorry, James.\"\n\nI do not know what she was sorry for.\n\nI have asked her since. She does not remember saying it.\n\n\u2014\n\nWe got to the second hospital at 4:02 AM.\n\nA nurse named Dolores took one look at her, put her in a wheelchair, and ran with her to triage. We have given her a temporary stoma, which means there is a bag attached to her abdomen that will collect her stool while the part of her colon we left behind heals. In about three months we will do a second surgery to reconnect everything. This is the rupture site. I want to walk you through how we get here, because most of the surgeons I trained with are not telling families about this.\"\n\nI sat down.\n\n\u2014\n\nHe stood in front of the screen with his hand on the image.\n\nHe said: \"Your wife's colon is a muscle. To do its job, that muscle has to contract and push waste through. To contract, it needs fuel. The fuel is a class of molecules called short-chain fatty acids. SCFAs.\"\n\nHe looked at me.\n\n\"SCFAs are produced by two specific bacteria that live in your wife's colon. The names of the bacteria do not matter for what I am about to tell you. What matters is that there are two of them, they live in her colon, and their entire job is to make the fuel her colon needs.\"\n\nHe pointed at the image.\n\n\"Now. GLP-1 medications do something to those two bacteria that almost no primary care doctor is currently warning patients about.\"\n\nI leaned forward.\n\n\u2014\n\nHe said: \"They starve them.\"\n\nHe said it quietly, like he was angry.\n\n\"The medication slows the entire digestive transit, which is part of how it works for weight loss. But that slow transit also changes what reaches those two bacteria. The compounds they feed on get suppressed. By month two or month three, in many users, those bacterial populations are already at a fraction of what they were before the medication started.\"\n\nHe tapped the screen.\n\n\"When the bacteria crash, SCFA production crashes. Your wife's colon lost the fuel it needed to contract. So waste built up. Pressure built up. The pressure has to go somewhere. The wall of the colon is not designed to hold pressure for weeks at a time. It thins at a weak spot. And eventually the wall gives way.\"\n\nHe paused.\n\n\"That is what I removed from your wife this morning. The wall that gave way.\"\n\n\u2014\n\nI want to tell you the next sentence Dr. Mwamba said because it is the sentence that will not leave my head.\n\n\u2014\n\nHe turned away from the screen and looked at me directly.\n\nHe said: \"Your wife is not the first GLP-1 patient I have done this surgery on this year. Most primary care doctors have not seen it yet. Most patients have not heard about it yet. To support the bile flow that the medication slowed. That is part of why the digestive system is sluggish.\"\n\nHe looked at me.\n\n\"Most products on the market have one of those three. I'm the daughter of a man who scooped white powder into orange juice every morning for twelve years, and I need to tell you what I found out too late to tell him.\n\nMy father was a bridge engineer for the state DOT for thirty-six years. Quiet man. Measured things for a living.\n\nThe MiraLAX showed up on his kitchen counter the year I turned 30. His GP had a phrase for it.\n\n\"This is your new best friend now.\"\n\nMy father wrote it down on a Post-it inside the kitchen cabinet. His engineer's block letters. NEW BEST FRIEND. Underlined once.\n\nI found it years later cleaning out the house. It's the one thing of his I kept.\n\nFor twelve years he scooped white powder into orange juice at 6:15 in the morning. Same scoop. He was 63. The GP said keep up the MiraLAX. Maybe add a little Metamucil.\n\nHe did. He did exactly what they told him.\n\nThe week he died, he didn't tell my mother how bad it had gotten. Pulled a card out of a drawer and handed it to me.\n\nDr. Aurelia Marchetti. Foundation Functional Medicine. On Maple Street.\n\nI took the card. Walked out without starting anything.\n\nThen sat in the parking lot for forty minutes before I could turn the key.\n\nI almost canceled the appointment with Dr. Aurelia twice. Two hundred dollars for an intake form that asks about my father felt like grief tourism.\n\nI drove there anyway.\n\nA converted craftsman cottage at the end of Maple Street. Wood floors. A window seat with a wool throw on it. Used to be somebody's dining room. Smelled like bergamot tea.\n\nThe receptionist offered me a cup. I drank it.\n\nDr. Aurelia came out herself. Not an assistant. Mid-fifties, gray bob, reading glasses on a beaded chain. She books one patient an hour. I was the patient.\n\nThe intake form was six pages. One whole page about my father.\n\nShe read all of it before she said a word. Then she read my colonoscopy from 41, the bloodwork, the years of nothing remarkable.\n\nShe put it down.\n\n\"I'm not going to send you for another scan. You've had them. They're normal.\"\n\nI started to say that was the whole problem. That everything was always normal.\n\nShe nodded before I finished.\n\n\"That's the cruel part of this. What's actually wrong doesn't show up on any of them. It didn't show up on your father's either.\"\n\nThen she said something I did not see coming.\n\nShe took her glasses off.\n\n\"I want to tell you something before we go any further. I spent twenty years of my practice sending people home for that same powder your father was on. 'This is your new best friend.' I said those words too. To a lot of women who looked like you.\"\n\n\"I sent them home with the powder and I told them we would monitor it.\"\n\nShe set the glasses on the desk.\n\n\"I did not understand what I was actually doing until I started looking at what the drug never touched. It took me a long time. I'm sorry it took me a long time. Your father's doctor was doing what he was trained to do. So was I.\"\n\nShe let that sit.\n\n\"I'm telling you this because I want you to know I know how that room felt today. I sat in a lot of those rooms.\"\n\nShe had a little notepad. She drew a slow line across it.\n\n\"A few times a day, your colon is supposed to squeeze. Hard. One strong contraction that sweeps everything down and out. That squeeze is what you feel as the urge. It's run by a little band of cells in the wall of the colon. Pacemaker cells. Same idea as the ones that keep a heart on beat.\"\n\nShe tapped the line.\n\n\"In someone like you, those cells have been wearing down. For years.\"\n\nI asked her how she could possibly know that. If no scan shows it.\n\n\"Because I've watched it walk through that door a hundred times. Women exactly like you. Every test clean. A little worse every year. And when researchers look at colons like that under a microscope, the cells that fire the squeeze are worn down. What wears them down is oxidation.\"\n\nI asked her what that meant.\n\nShe reached over and picked up an apple from a small dish beside her desk.\n\n\"Let me show you.\"\n\nShe cut it in half with a paring knife. Set one half on a small plate between us, cut side up. Left it there.\n\n\"Watch it while we talk.\"\n\nShe kept going.\n\n\"Deep in the wall of your colon, right against the layer where the muscle sits, are these pacemaker cells. Nobody's told you about them because you weren't supposed to know about them. When they work, you don't think about it. You just go.\"\n\nShe glanced at the apple.\n\n\"They are being damaged. Worn down. By free radicals your own gut has been overproducing for years. Processed food. Stress. A round of antibiotics here and there. All the ordinary things. They wipe out the good bacteria and leave the lining raw. And a raw lining throws off far too many of these corrosive little molecules. Day and night. They don't switch off.\"\n\nShe paused.\n\n\"The cells barely grow back. So the damage stacks up. Year after year. The squeeze gets weaker. Then it comes less often. Then it stops coming on its own at all.\"\n\nThen she said the line.\n\n\"And one day, you notice the urge is just gone.\"\n\nThe urge. The thing I'd stopped feeling at 48.\n\nShe nodded down at the plate. The cut side of the apple had gone soft brown while she talked.\n\n\"Nothing touched it. That's oxidation. Free radicals \u2014 the same molecules \u2014 breaking the flesh down from the inside.\"\n\nShe picked up a wedge of lemon from the dish and squeezed half of it over a fresh slice. Set it on the plate next to the brown one.\n\n\"Watch this one. It won't turn. That's what an antioxidant does. It steps in and neutralizes the free radicals before they can do the damage.\"\n\nShe set the knife down.\n\n\"It's the same chemistry that rusts a steel beam. It has been oxidizing the cells in the wall of your colon that fire the contraction. You can't see it on any scan \u2014 which is why every test came back normal while you got worse.\"\n\nThen, quiet.\n\n\"Your cells have never once gotten the lemon juice.\"\n\nShe let that sit.\n\n\"In my read, that's what's happening. Nobody can put a scan on it and prove it to you. Not yet. But it is the best explanation we have for why you are doing everything right and still getting worse.\"\n\nShe looked at me.\n\n\"It isn't your willpower. It isn't your fault. It's the modern gut, not you. The cells aren't dead. Take away what's corroding them and give the contraction a chance to come back.\"\n\n\"You are not broken. You did not forget how. The cells that run it have been wearing down. Quietly. The whole time your tests were coming back normal.\"\n\nShe let that sit too.\n\n\"That is why your father's came back normal. For twelve years.\"\n\nI put my hand over my mouth.\n\nNine years. A death certificate. A discharge summary I made myself read on a plane. And the thing that killed him had been sitting there under every clean test the whole time, and no one ever went looking for it.\n\nShe handed me a tissue from a wooden box on her desk and waited.\n\nI said, \"But they kept telling him more fiber. They told me more fiber too.\"\n\n\"Fiber is a raw ingredient. Your bacteria are supposed to ferment it. But the same diet that started this wiped those bacteria out. So the fiber just sits there and turns to gas. That's why it made you more bloated, not less.\"\n\nShe shrugged.\n\n\"You can't out-eat a contraction that isn't firing.\"\n\nI started to say something about the laxatives.\n\nShe got there first.\n\n\"A stimulant laxative \u2014 your senna, your Dulcolax \u2014 doesn't fix anything. It lashes the muscle into one forced squeeze. That isn't your body doing the work. That's your body being whipped into it. It works once. Then it quits. Then it needs a bigger dose.\"\n\nShe looked at me.\n\n\"Your father proved his colon could be forced for twelve years. He never once got to find out if it could work on its own.\"\n\nI couldn't answer that.\n\n\"And the MiraLAX,\" she said, \"pulls water in so what's already sitting there slides out. Not one of them stopped the damage, calmed the source, and helped the squeeze come back. All three, at once.\"\n\nShe said it plainly.\n\n\"The treatments failed you. Normal.\"\n\nBy year five they added magnesium citrate, three times a week. \"Just to keep things moving.\"\n\nAnd the bloating.\n\nBy the end his belly swelled every afternoon like he was carrying a basketball. Bacterial diversity. The acid-producing capacity of my gut. Inflammatory markers.\n\nThings no one had checked in six years.\n\nThree hundred and forty dollars out of pocket. I sent it in.\n\nTen days later we booked the follow-up.\n\nShe turned her monitor toward me. Color-coded bars across the screen, like a soundboard.\n\nShe pointed at the first one.\n\n\"This is your Bifidobacterium. These are the bacteria that make the chemical signal that tells your colon to contract. A woman your age should be up here.\"\n\nShe pointed higher. Then much lower.\n\n\"You're here. I normally see this in patients who've been on daily laxatives for years. You haven't started yet. Your bacteria thinned out from diet, stress, and aging alone.\"\n\n\"But my doctor said the constipation was the problem,\" I said.\n\n\"The constipation is the last thing to change,\" she said. \"Your bacteria have been thinning for a long time. Your doctor watched the number cross a line and reached for MiraLAX. But the shift underneath had been building far longer than the constipation had been obvious. Your bowel frequency is the surface. What I'm seeing under it ran ahead of it for years.\"\n\nShe let that sit.\n\n\"Here's the part nobody explained to your father,\" she said. \"Your colon isn't broken. It's a phone that stopped ringing. The line went quiet a long time ago, and your body's been sitting right next to it ever since \u2014 waiting for a call that hasn't come through.\"\n\nI felt sick.\n\n\"So what does the MiraLAX even do?\"\n\n\"It pulls water into your colon by osmosis. The waste moves from pressure \u2014 not because your muscles contracted. Your doctor sees that you went and says keep taking it. But laxatives move today's stool. They don't rebuild what stopped working. The output improves. The thinning underneath keeps going.\"\n\nAnd that's when I understood what happened to my father.\n\nTwelve years of managed output. Twelve years of bigger doses. His doctor said it was working the whole way down \u2014 while the root cause stayed unaddressed underneath.\n\nI told her.\n\nShe was quiet. \"That's unfortunately common. His gut looked like it was working. The bacteria that send the signal were thinning out underneath the whole time. That's the gap the laxative can't close.\"\n\nThere it was. The answer to the question I'd carried since I was 33, standing in a hospital hallway being told my father was gone.\n\n\"So is the laxative my only option?\" I asked.\n\n\"You have two paths,\" she said. \"Path one. You start the MiraLAX. You go more often at every checkup. But the thinning keeps going underneath. The dose climbs. Magnesium gets added. Then stimulant laxatives. The output stays managed. The cause stays unaddressed. That's the road your father was on for twelve years.\"\n\nShe paused.\n\n\"Path two. When the bacteria are healthy, those acids reach the receptors lining your colon. The receptors release serotonin. The serotonin triggers the urge, and the contraction. The waste moves through naturally.\"\n\n\"When the bacteria are depleted, the signal goes quiet. The muscles just sit there. Capable, but waiting. They're not broken. They're not getting the message. That's what constipation actually is. Not a stool problem. A signaling problem. The laxative never addresses it \u2014 your gut just leans on the bypass instead of recovering its own function. And the good news in that? Muscles that aren't broken, just quiet, can come back. That part is true.\"\n\n\"What about fiber?\" I asked. \"My doctor keeps saying more fiber.\"\n\n\"Fiber is the raw material,\" she said. \"If the bacteria that ferment it aren't there, more fiber does almost nothing. A lot of people with what you have don't respond to more fiber alone. That's well documented. That's not me being clever.\"\n\n\"And probiotics?
