more","cards":[],"body":{"text":"On a Tuesday in April, a woman I'll call Marion was admitted to my floor with the most ordinary word in medicine sitting at the top of her chart: constipation. We'll sort it out.\n\nThe next Tuesday she died of it, in Room 9, and I was the nurse who charted \"abdomen firm\" the shift before it turned.\n\nI've been a medical-surgical nurse for twenty-six years. I'm fifty-five. I am not a doctor. I'm not selling you my expertise, and I've never written anything like this in my life. But I have thought about Marion nearly every shift since April, and I've finally understood what I was standing next to that week. I need to tell you, because if you've read this far there's a decent chance I've been standing next to you too.\n\nLet me tell you what those six days actually looked like, because the chart doesn't.\n\nMarion was sixty-one. She came in for something else entirely \u2014 that part doesn't matter now \u2014 and somewhere in her intake was the line every nurse has typed a thousand times. Patient reports constipation. Hasn't gone in several days. Started on a bowel regimen.\n\nYou have to understand what \"bowel regimen\" means on a floor like mine. It's a ladder. Colace first. Then senna. Then a cap of MiraLAX. If none of that moves it, an enema. If the enema doesn't, magnesium citrate \u2014 the whole bottle. If that fails, someone puts on a glove. It is the most routine set of orders in the hospital. We run it on half the floor on any given night. Every rung of it manages the output. Not one rung of it asks why the body stopped doing the job on its own.\n\nMarion climbed the whole ladder in four days.\n\nHere's what nurses notice that the chart doesn't. It isn't the vital signs \u2014 hers were fine almost the whole way, which is exactly the problem. It's smaller than that. She stopped asking to get up to the bathroom. She got quiet in a way that isn't relief. When I pressed on her belly it was firm and it was silent, and a belly that's gone quiet is a belly that has stopped moving. I charted it. Abdomen firm, distended, hypoactive. I told the resident twice. It wasn't anyone's failure of caring \u2014 it was a Sunday, the floor was full, and constipation is the one thing every single person alive has had, so it's the last thing anyone takes seriously until it stops being constipation.\n\nBy Monday it was an obstruction. The wall gave out. The infection went into her blood, and she was gone by Tuesday morning \u2014 a week to the day after she'd walked in on her own two feet.\n\nI've gone back over that week more times than I can tell you. Whether I pushed hard enough. Whether a louder nurse gets Marion to a scan on Saturday instead of Monday. I don't get to know that. What I do know is that I was standing three feet away with all my training, and the thing that killed her had been sitting under a word I'd stopped reading years ago.\n\nThe part I can't put down is the hallway.\n\nHer daughter was out in the corridor outside Room 9 for most of that week, in the vinyl chairs we keep by the window. On the second day one of us asked her to bring in everything her mother took at home \u2014 we do that, it's called a medication reconciliation, you empty the whole cabinet into a bag and we sort it at the desk. She came back with a gallon freezer bag.\n\nI sorted it myself at the nurses' station. I still see it.\n\nMiraLAX. Metamucil. A bottle of magnesium and a second bottle of a different magnesium. Senna. Dulcolax. Milk of Magnesia. A dusty thing of castor oil. Align. Smooth Move tea. Prune juice. A jar of Triphala from some health store. Fiber gummies, two brands. There was a squatty potty at home, the daughter said \u2014 she just couldn't fit it in the bag.\n\nEvery one of them works on the stool. Softens it, bulks it, pulls water into it, forces the muscle to squeeze one time. Marion had a whole bag of things that manage the output, and she died of the one thing none of them were aimed at.\n\nThree days after the notice went around the unit, I got home off a night shift and opened the drawer in my own bathroom to find my melatonin.\n\nIt was Marion's bag.\n\nMiraLAX. The magnesium I take so I go every few days. The senna for when the magnesium doesn't. A box of Smooth Move I'm a little embarrassed about. Prune juice in the fridge downstairs.\n\nI'm going to tell you the part I've never said out loud at work. I've had this myself for a decade. I go every four or five days, on a good stretch. Somewhere in my forties the urge just \u2014 left. I don't feel it come on the way I did at thirty. I go because I make myself go, or because the magnesium makes me. I manage it the way nurses manage their own bodies: quietly, on my own clock, telling myself I'll deal with it properly when the floor slows down. The floor never slows down.\n\nI called her Marion in this letter to protect her. Standing at that drawer, I understood I could just as easily have called her me, a few years further along.\n\nSo I did the only thing I know how to do. I started asking questions, and I started reading.\n\nThe first person I asked was the GI attending \u2014 a woman I'll call Dr. Salinas \u2014 a few weeks later, on the floor. I asked her straight. How does a healthy sixty-one-year-old come in constipated and leave in a bag. Why does nobody catch this.\n\nShe didn't get defensive and she didn't blame anyone. She told me the honest thing.\n\n\"Because nothing looks for it,\" she said. \"There's no scan for it. No blood test, nothing on a panel. Constipation is the most common complaint there is, so it reads as the least serious thing on the board. We get six minutes a patient. In six minutes you rule out the emergency and you send them home with the regimen. Nobody's trained to ask what's actually wrong underneath it \u2014 because underneath it doesn't show up on anything we can order.\"\n\nThen she said the line I've kept. \"Most of them are fine, Carol. They get the enema, they go home, you never think about them again. Marion is the one in a few hundred you don't forget.\"\n\nShe's right. In twenty-six years I've watched hundreds of admissions start exactly the way Marion's did. Most of them do go home. She's also right that some of them don't \u2014 and there's no test on the whole floor that tells you in advance which is which.\n\nSo on my nights off, I read. Not testimonials \u2014 the actual research, the way I'd read up on any diagnosis I didn't understand. And I found the thing nobody had told Marion, or me, in twenty-six years.\n\nA few times a day, your colon is supposed to squeeze. One strong, sweeping contraction that moves everything down and out. That squeeze is what you feel as the urge. It's fired by a specific little band of cells in the wall of the colon. Pacemaker cells \u2014 the same basic idea as the ones that keep a heart on its beat.\n\nIn people like Marion, and like me, those cells have been wearing down for years. What wears them down is oxidation. Free radicals \u2014 produced inside your own gut in far too high a number \u2014 damaging the very cells that fire the contraction. And the reason they're overproduced isn't anything you did wrong. It's the ordinary modern stuff: years of processed food, stress, a couple of rounds of antibiotics. That thins out the good bacteria and leaves the lining raw, and a raw lining throws off these corrosive little molecules day and night. They don't switch off. The cells barely regrow, so the loss stacks up, year over year. The squeeze gets weaker. Then it comes less often. Then one day you notice the urge is just gone.\n\nI read that at my kitchen table at one in the morning, and I put the paper down and went and got an apple.\n\nI'd read that this is the same reaction that happens to a cut apple on the counter, and I wanted to see it for myself. I cut one in half and left it on a plate while I finished reading. Twenty minutes later the cut side had gone soft and brown. Nothing had touched it. That's free radicals, breaking the flesh down from the inside. Then I cut a fresh slice and squeezed lemon over it, and that one stayed white. That's an antioxidant \u2014 it steps in and neutralizes the free radicals before they can do the damage. It's the same chemistry that rusts a steel rail, running slow and quiet in the wall of the colon, on the cells that used to give you the urge without a second thought.\n\nHere's the honest part \u2014 the part Dr. Salinas taught me to say. Nobody can put a scan on this. There was no test I could have run on Marion to catch it, and there's none I can run on myself. It is not a proven picture of anyone's colon. It is simply the best explanation there is for why a body that did everything right slowly stops going \u2014 and for why every test comes back normal the whole way down, the way Marion's did, the way mine always have.\n\nAnd it finally explained the bag.\n\nFiber? Fiber is raw material your bacteria are supposed to ferment, but the same years that started this thinned those bacteria out, so the fiber just sits and turns to gas \u2014 which is why it made Marion more bloated, not less. You can't out-eat a contraction that isn't firing.\n\nThe stimulant laxatives \u2014 the senna, the Dulcolax \u2014 don't repair a thing. They lash the muscle into one forced squeeze. That's not the body going; that's the body being whipped into going. It works once, then it needs a bigger dose. Marion proved for years that her colon could be forced. She never once got the chance to find out whether it could work on its own.\n\nThe MiraLAX pulls water in so what's sitting there slides out. You go a little. Wet, full, still no urge \u2014 because the squeeze still isn't happening.\n\nEven the prescription version \u2014 the one a doctor reaches for when the drawer stops working \u2014 forces the contraction from a different angle. Which only confirms the contraction is the missing piece. It doesn't stop what's damaging the cells, so as more of them wear down it works less and the dose climbs. Nobody on that whole ladder is aimed at the free radicals. That's the one rung that was never built.\n\nWhich left the obvious question. If the answer is an antioxidant, what antioxidant actually reaches the gut and does this.\n\nThe research kept coming back to one \u2014 kombucha, the fermented tea. Not as a trend. As a genuinely potent antioxidant that gets to the gut and calms the very activity that overproduces the free radicals in the first place.\n\nSo I did what any tired, skeptical nurse does. I bought the bottles. Three weeks of kombucha off the refrigerated shelf, and I felt nothing.\n\nThen I read why. Heat is the one thing that destroys an antioxidant, and every shelf-stable bottle has been heated. Every \"live\" bottle is still fermenting in your fridge \u2014 making more alcohol and gas, not more of what you need. When they test these bottles, half don't even contain the acids printed on their own label, and one brand's active runs fifteen times stronger than another's. For the exact thing I was trying to get, the bottle is close to the worst form there is.\n\nI hadn't failed at kombucha. The bottle had destroyed it before I ever drank it.\n\nWhat I needed was the antioxidant kept intact, in a fixed amount, with the rest of the repair job handled too \u2014 the raw lining calmed, the good bacteria put back and fed. I built the list off the research. A concentrated kombucha extract for the free radicals. Slippery elm to settle the lining that's driving them. Two specific bacterial strains, each with its own trial in people with exactly this \u2014 one that helped people go more often, one that sped up how fast things moved through. And dandelion root to feed those strains so they actually take hold instead of washing straight out.\n\nI was ready to assemble it out of five separate jars, the way I'd assembled everything else in that drawer. Then I found one that had put all of it in a single berry gummy \u2014 one a day. It's called Jevawell. A cream-topped pouch, deep forest green, a small gold raspberry on the front. Twenty-nine dollars. A sixty-day money-back guarantee, which \u2014 I'll come back to that.\n\nI want to be honest about what the first week felt like, because I braced for the letdown I know by heart. The first week, nothing. I took the one gummy every morning with my coffee and waited to feel foolish.\n\nWhat came first wasn't the thing I was watching for. I slept through the night \u2014 but that could be anything, I wasn't counting it. The bloat that always showed up by evening wasn't there by dinner \u2014 could be placebo, I wasn't counting that either. I had energy at the end of a shift where I usually didn't. My husband was the one who said it, at dinner, before I'd let myself claim any of it. \"You didn't push your plate back tonight.\" I hadn't even noticed I'd stopped doing that.\n\nWeek two, on a Thursday, I went. On my own. No magnesium the night before, no bracing for it. I sat there afterward trying to remember the last time that had happened without a fight, and I couldn't.\n\nI didn't tell anyone. I wasn't sure it counted.\n\nAround week four the urge came back. The actual thing \u2014 my body telling me, instead of me telling my body. I hadn't felt that since my forties. And I hadn't touched the drawer in two weeks.\n\nHere's the part that got me. Everything I'd ever tried had a quit date. The MiraLAX quit on me at six months. Five years of things I sent her home with instead of an answer \u2014 the MiraLAX, the magnesium, the senna I added last month \u2014 better than a thousand dollars a year, to stand exactly where she started.\n\nThe last thing she said to me at that visit, I haven't been able to forget: I don't recognize myself anymore.\n\nThat is not a unique chart. That is the average chart of an English woman in my practice in her forties.\n\n\u2014\n\nThe second chart belongs to a 67-year-old Amish woman in the same town.\n\nShe first came to see me for prenatal care. She delivered three children in eight years, all with her midwife, and I caught the second one when the midwife was at another birth. She has come in twice for stitches when she cut her hand on a butcher knife, and once when her son broke his arm.\n\nShe has never been on a single laxative in her life. Not the MiraLAX, the magnesium, the senna, the fiber gummies, or the prescription drugs that fill the bathroom cabinets of women her age. She has never had a colonoscopy because she has never had a digestive symptom that warranted one.\n\nWhen I asked her \u2014 because by then I was asking everyone \u2014 she told me she goes every morning, on her own, the way the 47-year-old hasn't in years.\n\nI have hundreds of these charts. The English ones grow longer every year. The Amish ones, far more often than not, barely change.\n\n\u2014\n\nFor years I told myself it was the diet, until I actually looked at what the Amish eat. Full-fat dairy, bacon and eggs, white bread, pie at every meal, and pickled everything. They eat the exact foods mainstream nutrition has spent forty years telling Americans will clog them up for good.\n\nSo I told myself it was lifestyle, the hard physical work and the time outdoors. Then I looked at the women specifically. The grandmothers in their 80s aren't out plowing fields. Many of them sit and quilt and tend the kitchen all day, the same as my English grandmothers in their 80s. Same activity, same diet of pies and full-fat dairy \u2014 and yet it's my English grandmothers who end up in my office unable to go, far more than the Amish ones.\n\nSo I told myself it was genetics, that the Amish must have some founder effect that makes their guts work. The genetic studies have been done. There isn't one.\n\nSo I started asking. Patient by patient, visit by visit, what do you do that I don't see in any of my English patients?\n\n\u2014\n\nA 78-year-old Amish woman finally answered me.\n\nShe told me about something her family had made and eaten since she was a girl, the same as her mother and grandmother before her. A fermented drink, brewed in a crock in the kitchen, sipped every single day. Three generations of women in one kitchen, drinking the same sour-tasting thing for as long as anyone could remember.\n\nShe told me her grandmother had brought the practice over from the old country, and that it had come to America with the early Anabaptist communities. Her grandmother used to say every grandmother in America used to keep a crock like this going, until the doctors told them they didn't need it anymore.\n\nI asked her when she thought that happened.\n\nShe said her mother told her it was somewhere around the 1940s, when the drugstore started telling American women there was a pill for everything their grandmother's crock used to do.\n\nHer community didn't listen. The rest of the country did.\n\nThat was the difference. After 25 years, it was the best explanation I'd ever found \u2014 and the only one that fit everything I'd watched. It wasn't the diet, it wasn't the lifestyle, it wasn't the genetics. One population kept feeding their gut the thing it runs on, every day. The other threw it out and replaced it with a laxative.\n\n\u2014\n\nI went home that night and read everything I could find on what she had told me.\n\nThat fermented drink turned out to be a kombucha \u2014 and it is loaded with organic acids: acetic, lactic, gluconic, the exact same molecules your own gut bacteria are supposed to make. And those acids are not a vitamin or a fiber. They are the chemical signal that tells your colon to contract.\n\nThat's the part no one taught me. Your colon doesn't move on a schedule. It moves when it gets a signal. Specific bacteria in your gut ferment what you eat into those acids, the acids land on a receptor on your colon wall, the receptor switches on the squeeze that moves everything along.\n\nWhen years of antibiotics, processed food, stress, and laxatives starve those bacteria out, the acids stop getting made. The signal never gets sent. The colon never gets the message. So it sits there.\n\nThat's why my English patients say \"I've lost the urge\" and \"my body forgot how to go.\" Their bodies didn't forget. They stopped getting the text.\n\n\u2014\n\nThe average American medical school spends a handful of hours on the gut microbiome, out of four years of training and thousands of hours of clinical work. I had a handful of hours.\n\nAnd in all of it, not one professor taught me that chain. Not one taught me that a fermented food restores the signal. What they taught me \u2014 what the conferences and the drug reps and the free lunches taught me \u2014 was which laxative to reach for when a patient can't go.\n\nIt isn't a conspiracy. It's economics. Nobody needs to hide the fermentation research from you. They move you today and the next morning your body is just as silent as before.\n\nThey bulk the stool, which only helps if your colon still squeezes. Fiber and psyllium assume there are bacteria home to ferment them and a working muscle to push the bigger mass along. In a gut that's lost the signal, there isn't. So the fiber just sits there and bloats you. That's why so many of my patients tell me fiber made them worse.\n\nAnd they teach your colon to lean on them. The more you force the exit from the outside, the less your body does from the inside. The stimulant works once, then the next morning is quieter than ever. That's the trap that turns a one-week fix into a ten-year dependency.\n\nThree failures, built into every laxative on the shelf, drugstore and natural alike.\n\n\u2014\n\nThe Amish crock addresses all three.\n\nThe fermenting happens outside the body, in the crock, for days, before a single sip is taken. I went anyway. When their trip fell apart, they all frantically tried to reach me.\n\nI did not pick up the phone.\n\nI was in a stone village in the hills, on the third morning, drinking something I hadn't asked for.\n\nFor ten years, Tom and I traveled with the same five couples. Every year, somewhere new. I'm the one who planned it. Always. I found the houses, the restaurants, the flights. I booked everything, organized the itineraries, handled the problems when they came. That was my role. For a decade.\n\nTom died in March.\n\nEight months later, someone in the group texts that this year's trip is Portugal. Ten days. Lisbon, then the coast.\n\nI'd already started researching. I had a folder. The villas, the train schedules, a seafood place in Lisbon that took reservations a month out.\n\nThen the message came from Karen's phone.\n\n\"Hey Lynn. So we've been talking as a group, and we think it might be better if this year's trip stays a couples thing. Ten days is a LOT. The flights, the driving, the long dinners. We just want to make sure the trip runs smoothly for everyone.\"\n\nSmoothly for everyone.\n\nI read it twice.\n\nThen I called her.\n\nShe answered on the second ring.\n\n\"Karen. Talk to me.\"\n\nA pause.\n\n\"It's just, ten days is a long time. The driving, the late dinners, being on your feet all day. Tom always handled things for you two, and we just don't want you to be overwhelmed.\"\n\n\"Tom didn't handle things. I did. For all of us. For ten years.\"\n\nShe stopped.\n\nLong enough to answer the question without words.\n\nThen her voice shifted. Warm in the specific way that arrives just before a difficult sentence.\n\n\"Lynn, this comes from a place of caring. You haven't seemed like yourself in a really long time. You're always so tired. And honestly, at the last dinner you barely lasted past the main course. You kept getting up, you kept shifting in your seat. We just didn't think you could keep up with ten days.\"\n\nA pause.\n\n\"We didn't think you could manage it.\"\n\nI sat with that for a moment.\n\nI had planned every trip this group had taken for a decade. Found the villa in Tuscany that Karen still talks about. Booked the boat in Croatia that everyone calls the best day of their lives. Handled a canceled flight in Morocco for the whole group while everyone else stood around refreshing their phones.\n\nI did all of this. While also raising my son. While Tom traveled for work, sometimes for months at a time. I ran our household, his school, my career, and planned every trip, alone.\n\nKaren has known me for ten years.\n\nIn the last two of those years she'd watched me slow down. And she'd decided that was who I was now.\n\nAnd the worst part was that lately, I'd started to agree with her.\n\n\"Got it,\" I said. \"I hear you.\"\n\nI hung up.\n\nI'd already spent three weeks on their itinerary. The seafood place. A vineyard tour I'd found through a woman Beth knew. Walking routes through the old town that avoided the tourist crush.\n\nI sent Karen one message.\n\n\"I'll let you take it from here.\"\n\nThen I closed the folder and put my phone in a drawer.\n\n\u2014\n\nI called my sister Beth that night.\n\nBeth spent twenty-eight years as a flight attendant. International routes. She flew Lisbon out of Newark for the last eleven years of her career. She knows Portugal the way most people know their own kitchen.\n\nI told her everything.\n\nShe listened the whole way through. When I finished, she said, \"Lynn. You are not sitting this one out.\"\n\n\"I wasn't invited.\"\n\n\"That's not what I said.\" A long pause. \"Where are they going?\"\n\n\"Lisbon. Then somewhere on the coast.\"\n\n\"Then you go inland. Different Portugal entirely. They won't see a single one of you.\" She paused. \"There's a village I used to go to on my layovers. Two hours from Lisbon by train, then a taxi up into the hills. A little guesthouse run by a woman named Rosa. She's been running it alone since her husband died twenty years ago. She's eighty-something and she moves like she's fifty-five. I stayed there four times over the years and every time I left feeling like I'd put something back together.\"\n\n\"Beth.\"\n\n\"Lynn. Go. Eat real food. Sleep. Come back to yourself.\" She paused. \"Be the woman who planned every trip they ever took.\"\n\nI booked it that night. A small guesthouse in a hill village two hours from Lisbon. Six nights. A room with a view of the valley and absolutely nothing on the agenda.\n\n\u2014\n\nI'll tell you what I hadn't told Beth. What I hadn't told anyone.\n\nKaren wasn't entirely wrong. I did look tired. I was tired \u2014 bloated by every afternoon, heavy in a way sleep never touched.\n\nBut the tired had a cause. And it wasn't my age.\n\nFor over two years, my body had simply stopped going. Four, five, sometimes six days with nothing. No urge. No signal. Like the wire that's supposed to tell you it's time had been quietly cut. And everything that wouldn't move just sat there. By noon my waistband cut into me. By evening I looked pregnant, and I'm fifty-nine.\n\nThat was the \"tired\" Karen saw at dinner. The reason I kept getting up. The reason I kept shifting in my seat. The reason I barely lasted past the main course. Not my age. Not grief. A gut that had gone quiet, and a body carrying two years of what it had never cleared \u2014 heavy, foggy, drained in a way no amount of sleep could touch.\n\nI stopped eating before I had to be anywhere \u2014 food just piled onto a system that was already stuck. I'd turned down a weekend at the lake the summer before because I couldn't face a shared bathroom and a body that wouldn't cooperate.\n\nI had a drawer for it. Miralax, Metamucil, magnesium, Senokot, prune juice, a box of fiber gummies, an Align bottle I'd finished and refilled twice. Each one worked for a week or two. Then it stopped. Every single time.\n\nI'd been to the doctor. Twice. \"It's probably hormonal.\" \"It's grief.\" \"More fiber, more water.\" I drink eight glasses a day. I stopped going \u2014 to the doctor, and everywhere else.\n\nSo I'd gotten quiet. Started wearing loose dark clothes. Started being the one who offered to take the photo so I wouldn't be in it. I'd told myself this was just what fifty-nine looked like. This was just what grief did.\n\nAnd some small voice had started agreeing with Karen. Maybe I couldn't keep up. Maybe I was the tired one now.\n\nThat's the thing I carried onto the plane.\n\n\u2014\n\nThe village was the kind of place that doesn't perform for anyone. Stone houses along a narrow road. An old man sweeping the path to the church at seven in the morning. A woman who ran the guesthouse named Rosa, who was somewhere past eighty and moved like she was fifty-five.\n\nThat's the thing I couldn't stop looking at. Rosa was twenty years older than me and she put me to shame. Up before me every morning, carrying trays up a narrow staircase I got winded just climbing. Flat in her apron. Sharp. Quick. She'd lost her husband, run the place alone for decades, and she had more life in her than I'd had in years.\n\nOn the third evening she found me in the courtyard. She set a cup in front of me without asking. Not tea. Something cloudy and a little sour, with a smell like cider gone sharp.\n\nThen she looked at me the way you look at something you recognize.\n\n\"You sit down the way I used to,\" she said. Not unkindly. \"Careful. Like there is no room left in you.\" She tapped the cup. \"I knew that feeling once. A long time ago, it was mine.\"\n\n\"How could you know that?\"\n\n\"Your face. The way you carry yourself.\" She shrugged. \"I had the same look once. You don't forget it.\"\n\nI hadn't said a word about any of it. Not to Beth. Not to anyone. But something about a stranger in a courtyard, in a country where no one knew my name, undid me. And I told her. That my body had simply stopped going. Days of nothing. No urge at all \u2014 like a wire had been cut.\n\nShe didn't flinch. She just nodded, like I'd confirmed something she already knew.\n\n\"What is this?\" I asked, looking at the cup.\n\n\"My mother made it. From tea, and a living thing she kept on the counter \u2014 a pale disc that grew a new skin every week. You feed it, you drink a little every day.\" She tapped the cup again. \"It is the reason this body still works.\"\n\n\"What does it do?\"\n\n\"It wakes the gut up.\" She said it like she was explaining that water is wet. \"It feeds the part of you that gives the order to go. The order you stopped getting. Every woman in this village who lives a long time drinks it. My mother drank it every morning until the day she died. So do I.\"\n\nI must have looked skeptical, because she laughed. A real laugh.\n\n\"You Americans,\" she said. \"You take the pills that push it out. Push, push, push. And then nothing comes on its own, because you have taught the gut to wait for the pill. This does not push. It feeds the part that gives the order.\"\n\nThen she said something I haven't been able to get out of my head since.\n\n\"Your pills do the work your gut forgot how to do. So your gut forgets a little more. That is why you are all so tired, and so blocked. You ask louder every year, and your body answers less.\"\n\nShe wasn't a doctor. She had no degree on a wall. She was an eighty-something woman in an apron who had outlived everyone who ever doubted her, and she was describing, in her own words, exactly the thing my own doctor had shrugged at twice.\n\n\u2014\n\nI slept ten hours that night. I don't know if it was the air or just the first quiet I'd had in two years. But I lay in that room and thought about Rosa, eighty-something and unstoppable, and Karen's voice, we just didn't think you could keep up, and for the first time the two things didn't fit together the way I'd been letting them.\n\nMaybe I wasn't old. Maybe I wasn't grieving my way into someone smaller.\n\nMaybe I was just full of something I'd never cleared out.\n\n\u2014\n\nThe fourth morning, my phone was face-down on the nightstand.\n\nBy the time I picked it up there were twelve messages.\n\nKaren, three times. Two others from the group. My son Danny.\n\nI read them slowly, in the courtyard.\n\nThe seafood place in Lisbon I'd found needed the reservation I'd never passed along. They couldn't get in. The vineyard tour I'd arranged through Beth's contact had been released when my follow-up email never came. Nobody could work out the train schedule. Karen had gotten them on the wrong line out of Lisbon and they'd ended up an hour in the wrong direction. One of the rental cars never got picked up because nobody had the confirmation, which was in my folder.\n\nThe best photos from the whole trip, apparently, came from the hotel lobby.\n\nI set the cup down. I didn't feel triumphant. I just felt clear.\n\nI texted Danny back. I told him I was sorry to hear the trip had been rough. That I hoped they'd found moments to enjoy it anyway. That I was fine.\n\nThen I went to find Rosa, because I wanted to know exactly how to do this when I got home.\n\n\u2014\n\nI asked her how on earth I was supposed to keep a fermenting pot alive in a condo back home. She laughed at me.\n\n\"You don't need the pot,\" she said. \"The young ones, they make it now. A little gummy. One a day. The same sour, made to travel.\" She wrote a name on the back of my room receipt and pressed it into my hand. Jevawell.\n\n\u2014\n\nI tried to shortcut it anyway, when I landed. Of course I did.\n\nI knew what it was by then \u2014 kombucha. Fermented tea, the kind with the rubbery disc the brewers call the \"mother.\" I couldn't keep a pot alive in a condo, so I bought the closest thing I could find off the health-food shelf. Then a second brand. Then a third.\n\nIt did almost nothing. One was mostly sugar and fizz. One tasted like vinegar and gave me gas for a day. None of it did what Rosa's cup did, and I understood why. Hers was a living, concentrated thing, drunk every single day. A bottle off a shelf is mostly water, a little sugar, and whatever survived sitting on a truck. I lay there one night thinking, this is exactly how people give up.\n\nSo I did what Rosa had told me to do in the first place. I dug the receipt out of my bag and I ordered the gummy.\n\n\u2014\n\nIt came a few days later. A pouch of raspberry gummies. One in the morning, the way Rosa had her cup.\n\nIt wasn't a laxative. It didn't push anything. It was the modern version of what Rosa's family had been doing for generations \u2014 what grandmothers in villages like hers had done every morning for longer than anyone can remember, before anyone decided to swallow a pill instead. The same fermented sour Rosa drank, the organic acids her gut had always run on, made to travel and made to last. The young ones had added a little to help it along \u2014 a couple of live strains and some fiber to coax my own gut into making the sour on its own again \u2014 but the heart of it was the same thing that had sat on Rosa's counter.\n\nI'd read enough by then to know why it worked, and Rosa was right in her plain way. When that sour ferments, it makes a handful of organic acids \u2014 and those acids are the exact signal a colon uses to know when it's time to move. Years of laxatives, stress, antibiotics wipe out the bacteria that make them. No bacteria, no acids. No acids, no signal. No signal, no urge. That was my \"I lost it.\" It was never in my head. And it was never my age.\n\nWeek one, not much. A little more activity. Subtle but consistent. The sense that something was finally moving on its own.\n\nWeek two, a Tuesday morning, I went \u2014 on my own. No MiraLAX, nothing forcing it. The first time in over two years my body did it by itself. And by that evening, the bloat that had sat on me for two years was simply gone. I stood sideways in the mirror the way I used to look at Rosa. Flat. Not flatter. Flat.\n\nWeek three. The week that mattered. Because every supplement I'd ever tried, every protocol, they all crashed at week three. Two weeks of feeling better, then everything comes back. The bloating returns. The body goes quiet again. Hope leaves.\n\nNothing came back. The bloating stayed down. I was going on my own, like clockwork, every morning. The urge \u2014 the actual urge I thought I'd lost for good \u2014 was just there again, the way it's supposed to be. And the heaviness that had been sitting on me for two years was simply gone.\n\nWeek four, Beth came for dinner. She stopped in the doorway, coat half off, and looked at me.\n\n\"Okay \u2014 what's going on with you?\" she said. \"You've got your spark back. You haven't moved like this in two years.\"\n\nI hadn't changed my diet. I hadn't added exercise. I hadn't done anything except take one gummy every morning and let it do its work. The bloat was gone, the fog was gone, and whatever that does to a person, Beth saw it the second she walked in.\n\n\u2014\n\nKaren's birthday was in April. A dinner at her house. The first time I'd seen the group since Portugal.\n\nI walked in flat-stomached, rested, quick the way I used to be. I wore a fitted dress and I didn't offer to take anyone's photo.\n\nKaren watched me from across the room for a while. I could see her doing the math. Comparing the woman in front of her to the tired one she'd decided couldn't keep up four months earlier.\n\nToward the end of the night, she found me in the kitchen, away from the others, and pushed the door half shut.\n\n\"Lynn. I don't think I've ever seen you look like this. What did you do?\"\n\nFor a second the old reflex kicked in \u2014 give her the easy answer. The wine, the rest, a good few months. Keep it hidden, the way I always had.\n\nThen I thought about a stranger in a courtyard who hadn't kept it from me.\n\nSo I told her. Not all of it \u2014 but the part that mattered. A hill village two hours from the coast they never reached. An eighty-something woman who ran circles around me. A fermented thing every long-lived woman there has every morning. And, quieter, the thing underneath it: that my body had simply stopped doing the one thing it's supposed to do.\n\nShe went still. Then, lower: \"Can I tell you something I've never said out loud? I have the same trouble. For years. I never told a soul.\"\n\nThe woman who'd decided I couldn't keep up. Standing in her own kitchen, telling me she'd been hiding the very thing that nearly buried me.\n\nI wrote the name down for her.\n\n\u2014\n\nHere's what I learned.\n\nKaren looked at two years of watching me fade and decided that was who I was. She heard \"tired\" and \"bloated\" and \"can't keep up\" and turned it into a woman who needed to be left behind for her own good. And the worst part is I'd half believed her. I'd looked in the mirror and agreed.\n\nI wasn't past it. I wasn't too old to keep up. My gut had simply gone quiet \u2014 stopped getting the signal to move \u2014 and two years of everything that backed up was sitting on me like fifteen years I hadn't lived yet. The bloating, the exhaustion, the heaviness, the foggy head, the look that made my best friend of ten years decide I was finished. None of that was age. It was a body that had forgotten how to let go.\n\nI didn't come back from Portugal younger. I came back working again. What two doctors and a best friend had written off as my age, an eighty-something woman in an apron saw in one evening \u2014 a gut that had simply gone quiet.\n\nIf someone in your life has looked at everything you've carried and decided that means you need to be managed. If they've handed you a story about yourself you never agreed to. If you've done everything right and still bloat by dinner, still go days without going, still get told it's just your age, it's just grief, it's just what happens.\n\nIt might not be your age. And it was never your fault. The cruelest part isn't the bad weeks \u2014 it's the good ones.\n\nEvery so often my body hands me a good stretch. A week, sometimes ten days, where I go to the bathroom like a normal person. And every single time, I let myself believe it's finally over.\n\nNobody warns you the good weeks lie. The bad weeks, you brace for. The good weeks whisper: maybe you imagined it. Maybe your body's fine.\n\nThen comes a Tuesday where I'm kneeling on the bathroom floor at 6 a.m., heating pad on my belly, a plastic syringe of warm water in my hand \u2014 flushing myself out by hand just so I'll feel safe leaving the house. And the good week is gone like it was never real.\n\nMy name is Maureen. I work part-time at the community college library here in Athens, Georgia, and on Thursdays I run a memoir circle \u2014 a handful of older folks writing their lives down.\n\nIt started on a single Sunday in 2013. I can name the day. That morning everything worked the way it had my whole life. By that evening it just... stopped. And eleven years later my body still hasn't remembered how.\n\nAt first I thought it would pass. It didn't pass. It just got quieter and meaner.\n\nBy the end I was going once every two weeks. Sometimes longer. In between, I was bloated every hour of every day \u2014 not \"big dinner\" bloated, but hard and round and tight, the kind where you press your stomach and it doesn't give back. By noon I looked five months along. I started keeping a cardigan on my chair at the library and pulling it over my middle every afternoon \u2014 draft or no draft \u2014 so the patrons wouldn't see.\n\nBut the part that scared me most wasn't the bloating or the waiting. It was that I'd lost the urge completely. Not the pain \u2014 the signal. My body had stopped telling me it was time at all. I'd sit there out of habit, hoping, and nothing. Like a wire had been cut.\n\nSo I went looking for that wire myself.\n\nI took MiraLAX every morning with my coffee. Religiously.\n\nI drank sixteen glasses of water a day. A hundred and twenty-eight ounces, measured, every day, for years. If anyone ever told me to \"drink more water,\" I could have handed them the log.\n\nEighteen grams of fiber at breakfast alone.\n\nI quietly moved my fitted clothes to the back of the closet and stopped buying anything with a waistband.\n\nAnd I started dreading food. When you haven't gone in twelve days, every meal just piles onto a system that's already stuck \u2014 more bloat, more pressure, that full, heavy, almost sick feeling with nowhere for any of it to go. So I'd skip dinner before any morning I needed to feel halfway human. Eating became something I rationed.\n\nI dropped the Thursday circle from ninety minutes to forty-five, and told everyone my back was acting up.\n\nNothing dramatic. Just everything.\n\nNine days between movements. Then, after a year, fourteen.\n\nAnd there's a drawer in my kitchen I want you to picture, because I think a lot of you have one.\n\nMiraLAX. Metamucil. Magnesium citrate. Senokot. Dulcolax. Smooth Move tea. Psyllium. Prune juice. A box of Align that cost me thirty dollars a month for a while. A surgeon, and a bag, and my big sister crying in her car.\n\nThat was the dread I carried every day. This spring it got so bad that the woman who used to sing in our kitchen every Sunday morning stopped coming out of the bathroom at all.\n\nI'm not exaggerating.\n\nDiane is fifty-five. She's had a stubborn gut since her twenties \u2014 long before she met me. Over the years she tried everything you can buy. Miralax. Metamucil. Magnesium citrate. Stool softeners. Prune juice by the quart. More water. More fiber. Every senna tea and pill on the shelf.\n\nNothing worked. Not for long.\n\nFor a while, the Miralax was the closest thing she had to normal. A capful every morning in her coffee and she could count on going every three or four days. It wasn't good. But it was something. She called it her little miracle.\n\nThen, this spring, even that stopped working.\n\nAt first it was four days between. She'd add a second capful. \"Probably just a bad stretch.\"\n\nThen it was a week. She put the stool softeners back in.\n\nThen ten days. She was drinking magnesium at night and taking senna in the morning and still nothing. By evening she was so bloated she looked six months pregnant.\n\nThen it was twelve days.\n\nI found her on the bathroom floor at eleven o'clock on a Tuesday night. Knees pulled up to her chest. Crying, but trying not to make a sound so she wouldn't wake me.\n\n\"I can't do this anymore,\" she said. \"It feels like there's a brick in there. Like my body just forgot how to do the one thing it's supposed to do.\"\n\nThat was the night I stopped believing what we'd been told for twenty years.\n\nThe Doctor Who Didn't Listen\n\nI went with her to her next appointment.\n\nDr. Pruett had been her doctor for twelve years. Nice man. Never rushed us. But when Diane described what was happening, I watched him do the same thing every doctor before him had done.\n\n\"Constipation's very common at your age,\" he said, typing on his laptop. \"Are you drinking enough water?\"\n\n\"She drinks eighty ounces a day,\" I said.\n\n\"Fiber?\"\n\n\"She takes Metamucil twice a day. It makes her more bloated, not less.\"\n\nHe nodded. \"Sometimes fiber can back up in a sluggish system. Ease off it. Not the Facebook groups where everyone tells you to drink more water and eat more prunes. I wanted to know what was actually happening inside her \u2014 why a healthy woman who ate well and walked every day couldn't do something a toddler can do.\n\nI searched why some people \"lose the urge\" to go. Why laxatives stop working. Why every test comes back normal when someone is clearly not fine.\n\nMost of it was the same advice she'd already tried. Then I found a video from a gastroenterologist that said something no one had ever told us.\n\nIt wasn't about fiber. It wasn't about water.\n\nIt was about the signal.\n\nHe said your colon doesn't just ooze things along on its own. A few times a day it's supposed to fire one strong, coordinated squeeze \u2014 a real contraction \u2014 that pushes everything down and out. That squeeze is what you feel as the urge to go.\n\nAnd that contraction has a trigger. Tiny pacemaker cells built into the wall of your colon. They're the spark plugs. They fire the squeeze.\n\nThen he explained the part that made me sit forward.\n\nThose pacemaker cells can be worn down \u2014 oxidation.\n\nHe said years of processed food, stress, and antibiotics can turn your own gut into a place that throws off a constant stream of corrosive molecules \u2014 free radicals \u2014 and they slowly corrode the very cells that fire the contraction. Not all at once. Over years. And those cells don't grow back easily, so the damage just adds up.\n\nI paused the video and sat there in the dark.\n\nBecause it explained everything.\n\nIf the cells that fire the squeeze are rusting, the squeeze gets weaker. Fires less often. Then barely at all. You stop feeling the urge. Your body doesn't \"forget\" how to go \u2014 the part that sends the go-signal has been quietly corroding for years.\n\nAnd here's why it gets worse instead of better: every year a few more of those cells corrode, and there's less spark than the year before. Diane didn't have a bad month. She had a bad decade that finally hit bottom.\n\nThen he said the thing that made me angry:\n\nYou can't see it on a scan. A colonoscopy looks for blockages and cancer. It cannot see rust on cells that small. That's why every test Diane ever had came back \"normal\" while she got worse and worse.\n\nAnd suddenly every dead end made sense.\n\nFiber doesn't fix this. Fiber is just raw material your gut bacteria are supposed to break down. But the same modern diet that started the rust had already wiped out most of those bacteria. So the fiber just sits there and turns to gas. That's why more fiber made her more bloated, not less. It never touched the rust.\n\nLaxatives don't fix this. A stimulant laxative doesn't restore the squeeze \u2014 it whips the colon into one forced, artificial cramp. It's a jolt from the outside, not your colon's own push. That's why it works once, then needs a bigger dose, then stops. It does nothing about the corrosion. Diane wasn't getting better on Miralax. She was just getting shocked into going while the real problem kept rusting.\n\nProbiotics don't fix this either. Dropping more bacteria into the mix does nothing if the spark plugs that fire the squeeze are still rusting. She was in there, probably awake, probably hurting, probably wondering if this was just her life now.\n\nThe word the gastroenterologist kept coming back to was antioxidant - to neutralize the free radicals doing the corroding. Rust protection, for cells.\n\nI read for hours. I'm not going to pretend I understood all of it. But a few things came up over and over.\n\nThere's research showing those free radicals really do damage the pacemaker cells in the colon \u2014 and that constipated colons run these \"free-radical generators\" higher than normal ones. And there's research where scavenging the free radicals \u2014 brought the colon's contractions back.\n\nThen I found the part I wasn't expecting. An antioxidant neutralizes them.\n\nThe deeper problem was the gut that kept making them. Reseeding the good bacteria and soothing the raw lining calm that down over time.\n\nBoth problems. Which is how I ended up on the bathroom floor of my daughter's apartment in Tokyo at midnight, shaking and throwing up, while she stood in the doorway trying to remember the Japanese word for ambulance.\n\nOver constipation. The paramedics who came thought my bowel had burst.\n\nI'm 51, and I'd been constipated for ten years before I ever got on that plane. My daughter moved to Tokyo to teach English four years ago \u2014 said it would be for two \u2014 and this was the trip I'd been promising her ever since, so I wasn't about to let my own insides ruin it.\n\nIt started in my early forties. A little backed up one week, then most weeks, then once a week, then once every two and a shrug. By the end I was going maybe twice a month, and when I did it was hard little pellets \u2014 rabbit droppings \u2014 after half an hour of straining for almost nothing, and I'd stand up still feeling like there was a brick in there that hadn't moved.\n\nSomewhere in those years I lost the urge entirely. I couldn't tell you the day; it was already old news by the time I noticed. My body had just stopped giving me the signal.\n\nAnd I want to say this, because I know how it sounds: I did everything they tell you to do. Eight glasses of water a day, for years. I walked. I ate the vegetables, switched to the whole-grain bread back when whole-grain bread was the answer.\n\nAnd I had a drawer. Top right of the bathroom vanity, half-used bottles and expired packets and the wrappers I never threw out because throwing them out felt like admitting something.\n\nMiralax in my morning coffee every single day \u2014 the first doctor I saw for this actually told me it would be my \"new best friend,\" and he was right, it was. Metamucil, until I gagged on the orange grit and quit. Magnesium citrate that worked for a month and then needed a bigger dose and then I read it weakens the colon and got scared.\n\nPrune juice by the bottle. Smooth Move tea that just made the same boulder angrier. Senokot, which worked and then quit. Align for six months \u2014 the bottle emptied and nothing else did.\n\nPsyllium in a smoothie that tasted like wet paper, which my sister swore by, which made the bloating worse. I read later that fiber can do that. I read a lot of things later.\n\nAnd the whole time, I'd been checked. Colonoscopy, normal. CT, normal. Bloodwork, fine, fine, fine. Every one of them used \"everything looks normal\" as the reason to send me home with the same three words: fiber, water, Miralax.\n\nI'd get out to my car in the parking lot and just sit there and stare at the wheel. They told me I was fine for ten years. I knew I wasn't.\n\nBy the time I packed for Tokyo I'd stopped thinking about it the way a person should. I put a fresh box of Miralax in my carry-on. Three bottles of magnesium citrate in the checked bag, in case the airport scanner gave me grief. And a bulb syringe at the bottom of a toiletry bag, inside a sandwich bag, the way you pack a thing you'd rather your grown daughter never find.\n\nThe drawer had just become the suitcase. I'd been doing it so long I'd stopped expecting it to ever be any different. This is just how I am \u2014 that was the sentence I lived inside.\n\nI landed on a Tuesday. The Align \u2014 bacteria in a capsule that mostly don't take hold in a gut that's already that inflamed.\n\nEverything in that drawer, he said, had been managing what comes downstream of the damage. I went anyway. When their trip fell apart, they all frantically tried to reach me.\n\nI did not pick up the phone.\n\nI was in a stone village in the hills, on the third morning, drinking something I hadn't asked for.\n\nFor ten years, Tom and I traveled with the same five couples. Every year, somewhere new. I'm the one who planned it. Always. I found the houses, the restaurants, the flights. I booked everything, organized the itineraries, handled the problems when they came. That was my role. For a decade.\n\nTom died in March.\n\nEight months later, someone in the group texts that this year's trip is Portugal. Ten days. Lisbon, then the coast.\n\nI'd already started researching. I had a folder. The villas, the train schedules, a seafood place in Lisbon that took reservations a month out.\n\nThen the message came from Karen's phone.\n\n\"Hey Lynn. So we've been talking as a group, and we think it might be better if this year's trip stays a couples thing. Ten days is a LOT. The flights, the driving, the long dinners. We just want to make sure the trip runs smoothly for everyone.\"\n\nSmoothly for everyone.\n\nI read it twice.\n\nThen I called her.\n\nShe answered on the second ring.\n\n\"Karen. Talk to me.\"\n\nA pause.\n\n\"It's just, ten days is a long time. The driving, the late dinners, being on your feet all day. Tom always handled things for you two, and we just don't want you to be overwhelmed.\"\n\n\"Tom didn't handle things. I did. For all of us. For ten years.\"\n\nShe stopped.\n\nLong enough to answer the question without words.\n\nThen her voice shifted. Warm in the specific way that arrives just before a difficult sentence.\n\n\"Lynn, this comes from a place of caring. You haven't seemed like yourself in a really long time. You're always so tired. And honestly, at the last dinner you barely lasted past the main course. You kept getting up. We just didn't think you could keep up with ten days.\"\n\nA pause.\n\n\"We didn't think you could manage it.\"\n\nI sat with that for a moment.\n\nI had planned every trip this group had taken for a decade. Found the villa in Tuscany that Karen still talks about. Booked the boat in Croatia that everyone calls the best day of their lives. Handled a canceled flight in Morocco for the whole group while everyone else stood around refreshing their phones.\n\nI did all of this. While also raising my son. While Tom traveled for work, sometimes for months at a time. I ran our household, his school, my career, and planned every trip, alone.\n\nKaren has known me for ten years.\n\nIn the last two of those years she'd watched me slow down. And she'd decided that was who I was now.\n\nAnd the worst part was that lately, I'd started to agree with her.\n\n\"Got it,\" I said. \"I hear you.\"\n\nI hung up.\n\nI'd already spent three weeks on their itinerary. The seafood place. A vineyard tour I'd found through a woman Beth knew. Walking routes through the old town that avoided the tourist crush.\n\nI sent Karen one message.\n\n\"I'll let you take it from here.\"\n\nThen I closed the folder and put my phone in a drawer.\n\n\u2014\n\nI called my sister Beth that night.\n\nBeth spent twenty-eight years as a flight attendant. International routes. She flew Lisbon out of Newark for the last eleven years of her career. She knows Portugal the way most people know their own kitchen.\n\nI told her everything.\n\nShe listened the whole way through. When I finished, she said, \"Lynn. You are not sitting this one out.\"\n\n\"I wasn't invited.\"\n\n\"That's not what I said.\" A long pause. \"Where are they going?\"\n\n\"Lisbon. Then somewhere on the coast.\"\n\n\"Then you go inland. Different Portugal entirely. They won't see a single one of you.\" She paused. \"There's a village I used to go to on my layovers. Two hours from Lisbon by train, then a taxi up into the hills. A little guesthouse run by a woman named Rosa. She's been running it alone since her husband died twenty years ago. She's eighty-something and she moves like she's fifty-five. I stayed there four times over the years and every time I left feeling like I'd put something back together.\"\n\n\"Beth.\"\n\n\"Lynn. Go. Eat real food. Sleep. Come back to yourself.\" She paused. \"Be the woman who planned every trip they ever took.\"\n\nI booked it that night. A small guesthouse in a hill village two hours from Lisbon. Six nights. A room with a view of the valley and absolutely nothing on the agenda.\n\n\u2014\n\nI'll tell you what I hadn't told Beth. What I hadn't told anyone.\n\nKaren wasn't entirely wrong. I did look tired. I was tired.\n\nBut the tired had a reason, and it wasn't my age.\n\nFor over two years, my body had simply stopped going. I'd go four, five, sometimes six days without a real bathroom trip. By every afternoon my stomach was so bloated my waistband cut into me, and by evening I looked pregnant, and I'm fifty-nine. I planned my whole day around where the bathrooms were. I'd turned down a weekend at the lake the summer before because I couldn't stand the thought of a shared bathroom and a body that wouldn't cooperate.\n\nAnd it had stopped feeling like normal constipation. It felt like my body had forgotten how. Like the signal that's supposed to tell you it's time just wasn't firing anymore. No urge. Nothing. Days of nothing, then an hour on the toilet that ended in defeat.\n\nI was exhausted in a way sleep didn't touch. Foggy. Heavy. Carrying something I couldn't put down.\n\nI had a drawer for it. Miralax, Metamucil, magnesium, Senokot, prune juice, a box of fiber gummies, an Align bottle I'd finished and refilled twice. Each one worked for a week or two. Then it stopped. Every single time.\n\nI'd been to the doctor. Twice. \"It's probably hormonal.\" \"It's grief.\" \"More fiber, more water.\" I drink eight glasses a day. I stopped going.\n\nSo I'd gotten quiet. Started wearing loose dark clothes. Started being the one who offered to take the photo so I wouldn't be in it. I'd told myself this was just what fifty-nine looked like. This was just what grief did.\n\nAnd some small voice had started agreeing with Karen. Maybe I couldn't keep up. Maybe I was the tired one now.\n\nThat's the thing I carried onto the plane.\n\n\u2014\n\nThe village was the kind of place that doesn't perform for anyone. Stone houses along a narrow road. An old man sweeping the path to the church at seven in the morning. A woman who ran the guesthouse named Rosa, who was somewhere past eighty and moved like she was fifty-five.\n\nThat's the thing I couldn't stop looking at. Rosa was twenty years older than me and she put me to shame. Up before me every morning, carrying trays up a narrow staircase I got winded just climbing. Flat in her apron. Sharp. Quick. She'd lost her husband, run the place alone for decades, and she had more life in her than I'd had in years.\n\nOn the third evening she found me in the courtyard, and she could see it on me. The tiredness. The kind you can't hide from someone who's lived long enough to recognize it.\n\nShe sat down on the bench without asking and set a cup in front of me. Not tea. Something cloudy and a little sour, with a smell like cider gone sharp.\n\n\"You don't go,\" she said. It wasn't a question.\n\nI stared at her.\n\n\"How did you know?\"\n\n\"Your face.\" She shrugged. \"The heaviness. I know it. I had it once, when I was younger. A long time ago.\"\n\nI asked her what she meant, and she told me, in the slow, unhurried way of someone who has never once doubted a thing she does.\n\n\"Every morning of my life, I drink this. My mother made it. And her mother. The pot lived on the counter. You feed it, it ferments, you drink a little every day.\" She tapped the cup. \"It is the reason this body still works.\"\n\n\"What does it do?\" I asked.\n\n\"It wakes the gut up.\" She said it like she was explaining that water is wet. \"Every woman in this village who lives a long time drinks it. My mother went every morning of her life until the day she died. So do I.\"\n\nI must have looked skeptical, because she laughed. A real laugh.\n\n\"You Americans,\" she said. \"You take the pills that push it out. Push, push, push. And then nothing comes on its own, because you have taught the gut to wait for the pill. This does not push. It feeds the part of you that gives the order to go. The order you stopped getting.\"\n\nThen she said something I haven't been able to get out of my head since.\n\n\"Your pills do the work your gut forgot how to do. So your gut forgets a little more. That is why you are all so tired and so blocked. You are louder every year and your body answers less.\"\n\nI sat there and felt something turn over in me.\n\nShe wasn't a doctor. She had no degree on a wall. She was an eighty-something woman in an apron who had outlived everyone who ever doubted her, and she was describing, in her own words, exactly the thing my own doctor had shrugged at twice.\n\n\u2014\n\nI slept ten hours that night. I don't know if it was the air or just the first quiet I'd had in two years. But I lay in that room and thought about Rosa, eighty-something and unstoppable, and Karen's voice, we just didn't think you could keep up, and for the first time the two things didn't fit together the way I'd been letting them.\n\nMaybe I wasn't old. Maybe I wasn't grieving my way into someone smaller.\n\nMaybe I was just full of something I'd never cleared out.\n\n\u2014\n\nThe fourth morning, my phone was face-down on the nightstand.\n\nBy the time I picked it up there were twelve messages.\n\nKaren, three times. Two others from the group. My son Danny.\n\nI read them slowly, in the courtyard.\n\nThe seafood place in Lisbon I'd found needed the reservation I'd never passed along. They couldn't get in. The vineyard tour I'd arranged through Beth's contact had been released when my follow-up email never came. Nobody could work out the train schedule. Karen had gotten them on the wrong line out of Lisbon and they'd ended up an hour in the wrong direction. One of the rental cars never got picked up because nobody had the confirmation, which was in my folder.\n\nThe best photos from the whole trip, apparently, came from the hotel lobby.\n\nI set the cup down. I didn't feel triumphant. I just felt clear.\n\nI texted Danny back. I told him I was sorry to hear the trip had been rough. That I hoped they'd found moments to enjoy it anyway. That I was fine.\n\nThen I put the phone away and went to find Rosa, because I wanted to know exactly how to do this when I got home.\n\n\u2014\n\nI tried to do it myself first, when I landed. Of course I did.\n\nA store-bought kombucha from the health-food aisle. Then a second brand. Then a third.\n\nIt did almost nothing. One was mostly sugar and fizz. One tasted like vinegar and gave me gas for a day. None of it did what Rosa's pot did, and I understood why. Hers was a living, concentrated thing, drunk every single day. A bottle off a shelf is mostly water, a little sugar, and whatever survived sitting on a truck. I lay there one night thinking, this is exactly how people give up.\n\nBeth had been doing her own digging the whole time, because that's Beth. She called me a week later.\n\n\"I found what Rosa's pot actually is,\" she said. \"It's the fermentation. The sour part. When that tea ferments, it makes a set of organic acids \u2014 Rosa's grandmother just called it 'the sour' \u2014 and those acids are the exact signal your gut uses to know when to move. Years of laxatives and stress and antibiotics wipe out the bacteria that are supposed to make those acids. So the signal goes quiet. That's the 'I lost the urge' thing. It's not in your head.\"\n\n\"Okay,\" I said. \"So how do I get Rosa's pot without Rosa?\"\n\n\"That's the part,\" she said. \"A small company makes it as a daily gummy. One a day. That is a regular person's body talking to them. Slow gas. Slow ache. Bowel signal. Time to walk to the bathroom and read your phone.\n\nBy month seven, the warning was five minutes.\n\nBy month nine, it was two minutes.\n\nBy month ten, thirty seconds.\n\nThat is not a side effect of the medication.\n\nThat is something else.\n\nI did not understand what until the Tuesday after the kitchen.\n\nShe tried things.\n\nI want you to know she tried things.\n\nShe pounded Imodium when it got bad. We'll sort it out.\n\nThe next Tuesday she died of it, in Room 9, and I was the nurse who charted \"abdomen firm\" the shift before it turned.\n\nI've been a medical-surgical nurse for twenty-six years. I'm fifty-five. I am not a doctor. I'm not selling you my expertise, and I've never written anything like this in my life. But I have thought about Marion nearly every shift since April, and I've finally understood what I was standing next to that week. I need to tell you, because if you've read this far there's a decent chance I've been standing next to you too.\n\nLet me tell you what those six days actually looked like, because the chart doesn't.\n\nMarion was sixty-one. She came in for something else entirely \u2014 that part doesn't matter now \u2014 and somewhere in her intake was the line every nurse has typed a thousand times. Patient reports constipation. Hasn't gone in several days. Started on a bowel regimen.\n\nYou have to understand what \"bowel regimen\" means on a floor like mine. It's a ladder. Colace first. Then senna. Then a cap of MiraLAX. If none of that moves it, an enema. If the enema doesn't, magnesium citrate \u2014 the whole bottle. If that fails, someone puts on a glove. It is the most routine set of orders in the hospital. We run it on half the floor on any given night. Every rung of it manages the output. Not one rung of it asks why the body stopped doing the job on its own.\n\nMarion climbed the whole ladder in four days.\n\nHere's what nurses notice that the chart doesn't. It isn't the vital signs \u2014 hers were fine almost the whole way, which is exactly the problem. It's smaller than that. She stopped asking to get up to the bathroom. She got quiet in a way that isn't relief. When I pressed on her belly it was firm and it was silent, and a belly that's gone quiet is a belly that has stopped moving. I charted it. Abdomen firm, distended, hypoactive. I told the resident twice. It wasn't anyone's failure of caring \u2014 it was a Sunday, the floor was full, and constipation is the one thing every single person alive has had, so it's the last thing anyone takes seriously until it stops being constipation.\n\nBy Monday it was an obstruction. The wall gave out. The infection went into her blood, and she was gone by Tuesday morning \u2014 a week to the day after she'd walked in on her own two feet.\n\nI've gone back over that week more times than I can tell you. Whether I pushed hard enough. Whether a louder nurse gets Marion to a scan on Saturday instead of Monday. I don't get to know that. Twice. \"It's probably hormonal.\" \"It's your age. Eat more fiber.\" I stopped going.\n\nSo I'd gotten quiet about it. Started wearing loose dark clothes. Started being the one who held the camera so I wasn't in the picture. Started skipping the dinners where I'd have to sit through a meal feeling like a balloon. I'd told myself this was just what fifty-nine looked like.\n\nAnd some small voice had started agreeing with Mark. Maybe I wasn't up for it.
